🔄The interaction cycle

The important point is that Claude does not need to connect directly to the PaPM database or bypass SAP security.

A typical flow would be:

1️⃣User asks Claude

"Run an analysis of our profitability model and identify the top five cost allocations affecting Product A."

2️⃣Claude interprets the request

Claude determines that it needs information from the enterprise environment.

3️⃣Claude discovers/selects an MCP tool

The SAP MCP Server exposes appropriately defined tools and resources to the AI application. SAP describes these MCP tools as structured capabilities that AI agents can discover and invoke. (SAP Help Portal)

4️⃣MCP passes the request into SAP

The MCP layer can expose an underlying API, HTTP endpoint or RFC-based operation. SAP Integration Suite provides these mechanisms for creating MCP servers. (SAP Help Portal)

5️⃣SAP PaPM performs the controlled operation

PaPM remains responsible for the actual business logic:

Claude
   │
   ▼
MCP Tool
   │
   ▼
SAP Integration Suite
   │
   ▼
PaPM API / Integration Interface
   │
   ▼
PaPM Model
   │
   ├── Allocation Rules
   ├── Drivers
   ├── Calculations
   └── Results

6️⃣Results return through MCP

PaPM
  ↓
SAP Integration Suite
  ↓
MCP Server
  ↓
Claude
  ↓
Natural-language analysis

7️⃣Claude explains the result

Instead of returning a raw technical response, Claude could potentially explain:

"Product A's profitability is primarily affected by three allocation pools. The largest driver is indirect manufacturing overhead, followed by logistics and corporate support costs. The analysis suggests that the logistics allocation driver has the greatest sensitivity."

🧠 The real opportunity: PaPM becomes AI-accessible

This architecture creates an interesting separation of responsibilities:

Layer Responsibility

👤UserBusiness question
🤖ClaudeReasoning, interpretation and orchestration
🔌MCPStandardised AI-to-enterprise interface
🛡️ SAP Integration SuiteIntegration, security, policies and governance
⚙️PaPMFinancial/business calculations
📊Enterprise systemsSource data

SAP specifically describes its MCP capability as a way of exposing enterprise APIs and capabilities to AI agents through structured tools, resources, metadata and policies. (SAP Help Portal)

🔐Security and governance

A production architecture should not simply give Claude unrestricted access to PaPM.

Instead:

                 CLAUDE
                    │
                    ▼
             ┌─────────────┐
             │ MCP SERVER  │
             └──────┬──────┘
                    │
              Authentication
                    │
              Authorisation
                    │
                Policies
                    │
              Tool Controls
                    │
                    ▼
           SAP INTEGRATION SUITE
                    │
              API / RFC / HTTP
                    │
                    ▼
                 PaPM

SAP's current documentation describes OAuth-based authentication and policies for MCP access, with Claude Desktop able to connect using the MCP endpoint and the required credentials. (SAP Help Portal)

🚀What could a PaPM MCP toolset look like?

A conceptual PaPM-oriented tool catalogue could include:

MCP SERVER
│
├── 🔍 get_model_metadata()
│
├── 📋 get_function_definition()
│
├── 📊 get_model_results()
│
├── 🧮 execute_calculation()
│
├── 🎯 run_allocation()
│
├── 📈 analyse_profitability()
│
├── 🔄 run_simulation()
│
├── ⚡ analyse_performance()
│
├── 🐞 analyse_model_error()
│
├── 📚 get_model_documentation()
│
└── 📝 generate_model_documentation()

These should be regarded as illustrative tool names, not a claim that SAP currently supplies these exact PaPM MCP tools.

SAP Integration Suite allows selected API operations to be exposed as MCP tools, including defining their names, descriptions and input/output schemas. (SAP Help Portal)

🤖The future PaPM consultant?

The most exciting possibility is not:

"Claude replaces the PaPM consultant."

It is:

PaPM Consultant + Claude + MCP

                  PA PM CONSULTANT
                         │
                         │ Business expertise
                         ▼
                    ┌─────────┐
                    │ CLAUDE  │
                    │   AI    │
                    └────┬────┘
                         │
                    MCP TOOLING
                         │
                         ▼
               SAP INTEGRATION SUITE
                         │
                         ▼
                       PaPM
                         │
                         ▼
                  BUSINESS RESULTS

The consultant remains responsible for architecture, judgement, controls, business interpretation and solution design.

Claude becomes an intelligent interface for interacting with the available enterprise capabilities.

MCP provides the standardised bridge between the AI and those capabilities.

And PaPM remains the financial modelling and calculation engine.

That is potentially a very powerful combination:

🧠 Human expertise + 🤖 AI reasoning + 🔌 MCP + ⚙️ SAP PaPM = 🚀 Intelligent Profitability Management

SAP's architecture guidance describes MCP as an open protocol for connecting LLM applications with external data sources and tools, and SAP is actively participating in the broader Agentic AI Foundation ecosystem. (architecture.learning.sap.com)

SAP Help — How MCP Server Enables AI Integration
SAP Help — Connecting Claude to an SAP MCP Server

The SAP integration suite can be served by the SAP BTP platform and Joule.

 SAP Profitability and Performance Management (PaPM) is combined with Claude AI, SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), Joule and the Model Context Protocol (MCP)

This architectural configuration creates a pathway towards a conversational, intelligent and governed profitability-management architecture, where business users can ask complex questions in natural language, AI can reason over authorised enterprise context, MCP can provide a standardised tool interface, SAP BTP can provide enterprise integration and governance, and SAP PaPM remains the authoritative engine for profitability calculations.

The architecture can be summarised in one sentence:

Humans provide the business intent. Claude provides reasoning. MCP provides the connection. SAP BTP and Joule provide enterprise orchestration and governance. PaPM performs the calculations.

🧩 The architecture at a glance

The enhanced architecture introduces several important layers:

👤User / Consultant

⬇️

🧠 Claude AI

⬇️

🔗Model Context Protocol (MCP)

⬇️

☁️SAP BTP / Joule

⬇️

⚙️SAP Integration and API capabilities

⬇️

📊SAP PaPM

⬇️

🗄️ Enterprise Data Sources

The key idea is that these components have different responsibilities rather than attempting to make one platform perform everything.

1️⃣The User: Start with the Business Question

The architecture begins with a business user, finance professional, SAP PaPM consultant or solution architect.

Instead of navigating through multiple applications, the user could ask:

💬"Why has profitability declined for our North American customers?"

Or:

💬"Which cost drivers are having the biggest impact on Product X?"

Or:

💬"Run a simulation showing the effect of a 5% increase in logistics costs."

Or:

💬"Explain the allocation differences between this month and last month."

The important transformation is that the starting point becomes business intent, rather than technical navigation.

2️⃣Claude AI: The Reasoning Layer 🧠

Claude sits in the architecture as the natural-language reasoning and orchestration layer.

Claude can:

✅Understand the user's question

✅Determine what information is required

✅Interpret the available context

✅Select appropriate tools

✅Analyse returned results

✅Identify relationships and patterns

✅Explain the results in natural language

✅Produce recommendations

However, there is a crucial architectural principle:

Claude should not become the financial calculation engine.

If PaPM is responsible for a profitability calculation, allocation or simulation, the calculation should remain within the governed SAP environment.

Claude should reason about the result, rather than independently recreating the financial logic.

That distinction is fundamental to the architecture.

3️⃣MCP: The Intelligent Bridge 🔗

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides the structured interface between the AI reasoning layer and enterprise capabilities.

Instead of giving Claude unrestricted access to SAP systems, MCP can expose specific, governed capabilities.

For example:

🔧get_model_metadata()

🔧get_function_definition()

🔧get_model_results()

🔧execute_calculation()

🔧run_allocation()

🔧analyse_profitability()

🔧run_simulation()

🔧analyse_performance()

🔧analyse_model_error()

🔧generate_model_documentation()

These are illustrative capabilities rather than a claim that every named function is a standard SAP PaPM MCP tool.

The important architectural concept is the capability boundary.

Claude does not need to understand the entire underlying SAP landscape.

It needs to understand:

What tools are available, what they do, what inputs they require, what outputs they return and what permissions are associated with them.

That makes AI interaction significantly more manageable.

4️⃣SAP BTP: The Enterprise Control Plane ☁️

SAP Business Technology Platform provides the broader enterprise technology environment around the architecture.

This is where the solution can connect AI capabilities with SAP applications, integration services, APIs, identity, data and automation.

The BTP layer can potentially incorporate capabilities such as:

🔹SAP Integration Suite

🔹API Management

🔹Connectivity

🔹SAP Graph

🔹SAP Event Mesh

🔹SAP AI services

🔹SAP Build / process automation capabilities

🔹SAP Work Zone

🔹Identity and access services

The architecture therefore moves beyond:

AI → SAP PaPM

and towards:

AI → governed BTP capability layer → SAP enterprise landscape

That is a much more scalable enterprise architecture.

5️⃣Where Does Joule Fit? 🤖

Joule introduces an important SAP-native conversational and orchestration dimension.

In the conceptual architecture, Joule acts as the SAP-side AI assistant and enterprise interaction layer, while Claude provides the external LLM reasoning capability.

This distinction is important.

Joule should not automatically be interpreted as simply being a user interface for Claude, nor should the architecture imply that SAP has productised a direct "Joule-to-Claude-to-PaPM" connector.

Instead, the diagram represents a reference architecture in which SAP BTP and Joule capabilities can participate in the orchestration of enterprise AI interactions, while Claude represents the chosen external reasoning model.

The precise implementation would depend on the SAP services, APIs, identity architecture and integration patterns available in the customer's environment.

6️⃣SAP PaPM: The Financial Calculation Authority 📊

At the heart of the architecture remains SAP PaPM.

This is extremely important.

PaPM can continue to provide the controlled environment for:

📌Profitability calculations

📌Allocations

📌Cost modelling

📌Revenue analysis

📌Drivers

📌Simulations

📌Financial results

📌Performance analysis

📌Business rules

📌Calculation models

The AI layer does not replace this.

Instead, it makes the capabilities of the PaPM environment more accessible.

This creates a powerful division of responsibility:

AI understands the question.

PaPM performs the calculation.

AI explains the result.

The human makes the business decision.

7️⃣Enterprise Data: Connecting the Bigger Picture 🗄️

PaPM rarely exists in isolation.

The architecture therefore recognises the wider enterprise data ecosystem.

Potential sources can include:

🏢SAP S/4HANA

📈SAP BW/4HANA

☁️SAP Datasphere

🗃️ Databases

🔌APIs and services

📄Documents

🌐External enterprise systems

These sources can provide the information required by PaPM and, where appropriately governed, contextual information required by AI.

The critical principle is:

Claude should not bypass enterprise data governance simply because an AI interface exists.

Access should continue through authorised enterprise pathways.

8️⃣The End-to-End Interaction Flow 🔄

Consider a simple example.

Step 1 — The user asks:

"Analyse our allocation model and identify the biggest cost drivers."

Step 2 — Claude interprets the request 🧠

Claude determines that it needs:

 

  • Allocation information
  • Model metadata
  • Cost-driver information
  • Relevant results

 

Step 3 — Claude selects an MCP capability 🔗

The appropriate MCP tools are selected.

Step 4 — The request enters the SAP BTP environment ☁️

The enterprise integration layer can authenticate the request, apply policies and determine whether the requested capability is authorised.

Step 5 — PaPM performs the operation ⚙️

PaPM retrieves or calculates the required information using its existing business logic.

Step 6 — Results return through the governed architecture 📊

The results are passed back through the controlled integration pathway.

Step 7 — Claude interprets the results 💬

Claude can explain:

 

  • The largest cost drivers
  • The biggest changes
  • Potential causes
  • Relationships between drivers
  • Areas requiring investigation

 

The user receives an understandable business explanation rather than simply a technical data extract.

9️⃣Security and Governance 🛡️

This is perhaps the most important part of the entire architecture.

An enterprise AI system connected to financial systems cannot simply rely on the LLM to "do the right thing."

Governance needs to exist outside the model.

The architecture therefore introduces multiple control layers.

🔐Authentication

Who is requesting the operation?

👤Authorisation

What is that user or AI client allowed to access?

📜Policies

Which data and capabilities can be exposed?

🔧Tool controls

Which MCP tools can the agent invoke?

📊Monitoring

What happened during the interaction?

📝Audit logging

Who requested the action, which tool was used, what parameters were supplied and what happened?

This produces a much stronger enterprise model than simply connecting a chatbot to an SAP backend.

🔟Not All AI Actions Should Have the Same Level of Autonomy

One of the most interesting aspects of the architecture is that AI capabilities can be divided into maturity levels.

Level 1 — READ 👀

Retrieve approved information.

Example:

"Show me profitability for Product X."

Low relative risk.

Level 2 — ANALYSE 🔎

Interpret existing information.

Example:

"Why did profitability decline?"

Higher value, but still largely read-only.

Level 3 — SIMULATE 🧮

Run controlled scenarios.

Example:

"What happens if logistics costs increase by 5%?"

Requires parameter controls and appropriate authorisation.

Level 4 — PROPOSE 💡

Generate recommendations.

Example:

"Which customers should we investigate based on declining margins?"

Human review becomes increasingly important.

Level 5 — EXECUTE ⚡

Perform an enterprise action.

Example:

"Execute the approved allocation process."

This should require significantly stronger controls, authorisation and potentially explicit human approval.

1️⃣1️⃣Why This Architecture Matters for SAP PaPM Consultants

This architecture could fundamentally change the role of the PaPM consultant.

Traditionally, the consultant focuses on:

📐Model design

⚙️Functions

🔄Allocations

📊Calculations

🧪 Testing

📋Documentation

🚀Implementation

With AI and MCP, another discipline emerges:

AI-enabled PaPM architecture

The consultant may increasingly need to define:

🔹Which PaPM capabilities should be exposed to AI?

🔹What should each tool do?

🔹What parameters should be allowed?

🔹What data should be returned?

🔹Which users can invoke the tool?

🔹Which operations require approval?

🔹How should results be explained?

🔹How should AI outputs be tested?

This creates a new intersection between:

SAP PaPM + Enterprise Architecture + AI Engineering + Governance

1️⃣2️⃣The Future of PaPM Could Be Conversational 💬

Imagine a future PaPM environment where a consultant can ask:

"Show me the five largest changes in customer profitability this quarter."

Then:

"Explain the first one."

Then:

"Which allocation drivers contributed to the change?"

Then:

"Run a controlled simulation assuming logistics costs increase by 3%."

Then:

"Compare that scenario with the current result."

The interaction becomes conversational.

The user does not necessarily need to know the underlying technical sequence.

The AI orchestrates the interaction.

MCP provides structured capabilities.

BTP governs the enterprise interaction.

PaPM performs the calculations.

1️⃣3️⃣The Most Important Principle

The architecture can ultimately be reduced to six principles:

🧠 Claude — Reason

🔗MCP — Connect

☁️BTP — Integrate

🤖Joule — Assist and orchestrate within the SAP experience

📊PaPM — Calculate

👨💼Human — Decide

This separation is what makes the architecture interesting.

It does not attempt to make AI replace SAP PaPM.

It attempts to make SAP PaPM intelligently accessible.

🚀Conclusion

The combination of SAP PaPM, Claude AI, MCP, SAP BTP and Joule presents an interesting architectural direction for the next generation of profitability and performance management.

The real opportunity is not simply:

"Let's put AI on top of PaPM."

The opportunity is:

"Let's create a governed capability architecture through which AI can safely understand, access, analyse and explain PaPM capabilities."

That could transform how consultants and business users interact with profitability models.

Instead of navigating technical complexity first and asking business questions second, the process can increasingly begin with the business question.

Ask → Understand → Connect → Calculate → Explain → Decide.

And perhaps the future of intelligent profitability management can be summarised as:

Human expertise + Claude AI reasoning + MCP interoperability + SAP BTP governance + Joule + SAP PaPM = intelligent, secure and governed business insight. 🚀

I would be very interested to hear from the SAP community:

Would you trust an AI assistant to analyse your PaPM models?

And more importantly:

What PaPM capability would you want to expose through MCP first?

entry.title: Meet Flow and Model Flow: New Rule-Based Posting Functions in SAP PaPM Universal Model
entry.content:
Hi everyone! Welcome to this blog post covering one of the latest innovations in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model (SAP PaPM Cloud UM).

Introducing Flow and Model Flow: two new functions designed to help organizations transform data more efficiently through configurable, rule-based processing.

In this blog post, we'll explore how these new functions work, their key concepts, and how they can help you streamline complex transformation scenarios with greater flexibility and efficiency.

 

Flow: Your Automated Posting Generator

Think of the Flow function as an automated posting engine. You give it financial transaction data, define how those transactions should be transformed, and it produces a set of output postings. A classic example is intercompany (IC) elimination: when companies within the same group trade with each other, those transactions must be cancelled out when preparing consolidated financial statements. Flow automates that logic — it reads the IC transactions, applies your elimination rules, and writes the offsetting postings automatically.

What Flow Can Do:

Base Fields — the front-door filter: Before any rule runs, Base Fields narrow down which input records even enter the function. You can filter by field value, or by hierarchy selection. A hierarchy-based filter covers an entire organizational division or account group, and automatically includes any new members added to that hierarchy later. Records that do not match are excluded silently before any rule logic executes run. You can also use a formula to assign a default value to a Line Assignment before the rule is processed.

Rules and Conditions: Rules are the core of Flow. Each rule has two parts: a Condition (when does this rule apply?) and one or more Lines (what does the output look like?). Conditions support three types: Value Filter, Field Comparison, and Hierarchy.

Fan-Out Line Assignments: A single rule can contain multiple Lines, each with its own field assignments. Every Line produces one separate output row per matching input record. This fan-out pattern means you can generate a debit posting and an offsetting credit posting from a single transaction in one step.

Input of Flow:

Rule Settings displays two lines:

Output of Flow:
Since two lines were configured, the Flow creates two output lines for each matching input record. In the input data, there are two records with Account 5000. As a result, the Flow generates two output lines for each of these records, producing a total of four rows in the result.

Rule Levels — parallel and sequential execution: Rules are assigned to numbered Levels that control execution order. Rules at the same Level run in parallel against the same input. Rules at a higher Level run sequentially after all lower Levels complete, receiving the previous Level's output as new input. This lets you chain transformations — for example, tagging records at Level 1, aggregating them at Level 2, and applying a consolidation rate at Level 3 — without any custom orchestration logic.

Dynamic Rules: Mark rules as templates and import large volumes of rules from a CSV file via Manage Activities — useful for managing high-volume elimination logic without configuring each rule manually.

A Simple Example

To illustrate, imagine you have revenue records by region and you want to create offsetting postings with a negative amount:

INPUT

ACCOUNT

REGION

AMOUNT

REVENUE

EUROPE

10,000

REVENUE

AMERICA

5,000

SALARY

EUROPE

8,000


You configure a Base Field to filter only records where ACCOUNT = REVENUE, and define two rules — one for each region — that assign POSTING_AMOUNT = AMOUNT × -1.

RESULT

ACCOUNT

REGION

POSTING_AMOUNT

REVENUE

EUROPE

-10,000

REVENUE

AMERICAS

-5,000


The SALARY record is not processed by the rules because it does not meet the configured Base Field selection criteria. The two rules run in parallel since they share the same level.

Where the Results Go: Result Model Function

By default, Flow output is available in the Data Screen for that run. To make results available to downstream functions, configure a Result Model Function — a Model Entity that acts as the persistent write-back target for Flow's output.

With a Result Model Function in place:

  • Output postings are stored as standard Model Entity records
  • Other functions (Allocation, Derivation, another Flow) can read the stored postings as their input, enabling multi-step consolidation pipelines
  • Each re-run replaces the previous results, so the Model Entity always reflects the latest execution

This pattern decouples the computation (Flow) from the consumption (downstream functions), making the pipeline easier to audit, re-run independently, and version.

Note: The Result Model Function is available for Flow only. Model Flow does not support write-back.

 

Model Flow: A Live Preview of Your Rule Logic

The Model Flow function shares the same configuration interface and rule engine as Flow, but it works differently under the hood. Instead of running as a procedure that you run, Model Flow activates as a read-only analytical view — always live, always current.

Every time you open Show Data, the rules are re-evaluated against the current input data on the spot. There is no run step, no stored results, and no snapshot. This makes Model Flow ideal for pre-run validation: check exactly what your rules would produce with today's data before committing to a production run.

 

Flow vs. Model Flow — Key Differences

Feature

🚀Flow

🔍Model Flow

Execution Model

Process that generates a point-in-time snapshot of results

Read-only view that is re-evaluated on demand

Results

Results can be generated and optionally stored using a Result Model Function

Always-current view without storing results

Result Model Function

✅Supported

❌Not Supported

Hierarchy Conditions

✅Supported in Base Fields and Rule Conditions

✅Supported in Base Fields and Rule Conditions

Dynamic Rules

✅Supported

❌Not Supported

Typical Use

Production runs, period-end eliminations, and postings consumed by downstream functions

Pre-run validation to simulate rule results against live data before a production run

Shared Capabilities

Base Fields, Predicates, Rules, Rule Levels, Condition Types, and Fan-Out Line Assignments

Base Fields, Predicates, Rules, Rule Levels, Condition Types, and Fan-Out Line Assignments

💡Quick Tip
Use Model Flow to validate and analyze rule behavior against current data. Use Flow when you are ready to run the process and generate results.

In Plain Terms

Model Flow is a live preview window into your rule logic — always current, never storing anything. Flow is a controlled execution — you decide when it runs, and optionally where the results go.

Both functions are available in Universal Model. For the full configuration guide, see the SAP Application Help:

  • Flow
  • Model Flow

entry.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: Introducing the AI Conversation Monitor
entry.content:
Hello, SAP Community members!

 

If you manage SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model and your organization is using Joule, this one is for you.

 

As Joule becomes a bigger part of how users work with data and reports, administrators face a practical question: what are users actually discussing with the AI? When a conversation produces an unexpected result, or when a compliance team asks for a record of AI interactions, where do you go?

 

That changes with the AI Conversation Monitor. Available via the System submenu, it gives administrators a full view of every Joule conversation in the system. You can read the content of any conversation, download conversations as ZIP archives for audit or offline review, upload previously downloaded archives to restore conversations, and delete conversations along with all associated messages and files.

 

Why Does the AI Conversation Monitor Matter?

 

Joule conversations contain real business context. The prompts show how users are thinking through their data. The AI responses influenced decisions. The uploaded files were part of active analysis. Without a way to see and manage these conversations from one place, administrators have limited visibility into how AI is being used and no clean path for compliance reviews or data lifecycle management.

 

Note: Joule users are informed up front that administrators can access their conversations. The AI Notice within the Joule panel displays: "Joule is powered by generative AI and all output should be reviewed before use. System administrators can access conversations for security, compliance, troubleshooting, or quality assurance purposes. Please do not enter any sensitive personal data, and avoid entering any other personal data you do not wish to be processed. Learn more in the Joule Data Protection and Privacy."

Before You Begin

 

  • Downloading, uploading, and deleting conversations each produce a separate log entry in the Application Monitor and the Process Monitor. Each entry includes a dedicated Joule run type and conversation IDs of all affected conversations. These entries persist even after conversations are deleted.
  • The 400 MB size limit applies to uploads only. Downloads have no cap. The system always produces a single ZIP archive regardless of how many conversations you select or their total size. If you plan to re-upload a downloaded archive larger than 400 MB, split it first.

 

Access and Required Roles

 

The AI Conversation Monitor is available to administrators with one of the following roles:

  • AI_CONVERSATION_ALL: Full access to all toolbar actions, including Download, Upload, and Delete.
  • SYSTEM_USER_ALL: Legacy role with the same access as AI_CONVERSATION_ALL.
  • AI_CONVERSATION_READ: Can view the conversation list, open the content panel, and download conversations. Cannot upload or delete.

 

Administrators without any of these roles will see the AI Conversation Monitor greyed out in the System menu. Navigating to the screen directly returns a 403 Forbidden error.

 

Note: For details on role templates in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model, see Role Templates in Standard Model  on the SAP Help Portal.

 

Meet the AI Conversation Monitor

 

Navigate to Menu > System > AI Conversation Monitor.

 

 

The screen has three areas:

  1. The Conversation List shows a tabular view of all recorded Joule conversations. Each row has six columns: Conversation ID, Title, Local Timestamp, User, Number of Messages, and Number of Files. Sorting, filtering, column arrangement, and grouping work the same way as on other monitors in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model. If you have used the Application Monitor or Process Monitor, the table will feel familiar.
  2. The Conversation Content Panel opens on the same screen when you select a row. It shows all prompts and Joule responses in chronological order, plus any files uploaded during that conversation. Each file is a downloadable link, so you can retrieve individual attachments without exporting the full archive. Close the panel with the X button at the top right, the Esc key, or by clicking outside it.

 

The Message Log sits at the bottom of the screen in the same format used on other SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model screens like Content Management and Process Scheduler. After each download, upload, and deletion, the result appears here, so you can confirm it without leaving the screen.

 

Toolbar Actions

 

The header toolbar has three sections: General, Edit, and Layout.

 

The General section has the Refresh button, which reloads the conversation list without reloading the browser.

 

The Edit section has three action buttons:

1.       Download Conversations

 

Select one or more rows and click Download Conversations to export them as a single timestamped ZIP archive. The archive contains one folder per conversation. Each folder holds a JSON file with full conversation content and metadata (Conversation ID, Title, Local Timestamp, User, and all messages), plus all files uploaded during that conversation.

 

Important:

  • The Download button is not available when no row is selected.
  • Download is all-or-nothing. Either all selected conversations are packaged successfully, or the entire operation fails. There is no partial download.
  • The operation is logged in the Application Monitor and Process Monitor under the Joule Conversation Download run type.
  • When you start a download, the system displays toast notifications to indicate the progress and outcome of the operation and records the result in the Message Log. For single downloads, the Message Log contains the corresponding Conversation ID, while for bulk downloads, it directs you to the Application Monitor, where you can view the complete list of downloaded items.

 

 

2.       Upload Conversations

 

Choose Upload Conversations to restore previously downloaded conversations from a ZIP archive. The Upload button is always available, regardless of row selection.

 

The system checks the archive and restores only conversations that are not already in the system. If a Conversation ID already exists, that conversation is skipped rather than overwritten. If part of a conversation is corrupted (a single message or file, for example), that part is skipped and the rest of the conversation is still imported. When the upload finishes, the Message Log shows a summary of how many conversations were imported and how many were skipped.

 

Important:

  • Upload is available to AI_CONVERSATION_ALL and SYSTEM_USER_ALL only. Administrators with AI_CONVERSATION_READ cannot access this action.
  • ZIP files larger than 400 MB are rejected. Split the archive before uploading.
  • The operation is logged in the Application Monitor and Process Monitor under the Joule Conversation Upload run type.
  • When you start an upload, the system displays toast notifications to indicate the progress and outcome of the operation and records the result in the Message Log. For single uploads, the Message Log contains the corresponding Conversation ID, while for bulk uploads, it directs you to the Application Monitor for the complete list. If some conversations were skipped or partially imported, the Message Log also shows the imported and skipped counts.

 

3.       Delete Conversations

 

Select one or more rows and choose Delete Conversations from the header toolbar. A confirmation dialog opens before the deletion is performed, allowing you to review the action and either proceed with or cancel the operation.

Important:

  • Conversation deletion is available to users with AI_CONVERSATION_ALL and SYSTEM_USER_ALL role only. Administrators with AI_CONVERSATION_READ role cannot delete conversations.
  • Deletion is permanent. All associated messages and files are removed and cannot be recovered.
  • The operation is logged in the Application Monitor and Process Monitor under the Joule Conversation Deletion run type.
  • Audit log entries in the Application Monitor persist after deletion. A deleted conversation remains traceable by its Conversation ID.
  • When you start a deletion, the system displays toast notifications to indicate the progress and outcome of the operation and records the result in the Message Log. For single deletions, the Message Log contains the corresponding Conversation ID, while for bulk deletions, it directs you to the Application Monitor, where you can view the complete list of deleted items.

 

Layout

The AI Conversation Monitor supports full layout management. Save private or public layouts, switch between them, set a default, and rename or delete your own layouts, consistent with other monitor screens.

End-to-End Scenario: From Joule Session to Archived Record

Here is what a typical oversight and archiving workflow looks like.

  1. A team member uses Joule for a series of AI-assisted queries. The conversation is recorded automatically and shows up in the AI Conversation Monitor for administrators with the appropriate role.
  2. Navigate to Menu > System > AI Conversation Monitor. The conversation is in the list with its Conversation ID, Title, Local Timestamp, originating user, and message and file counts.
  3. Select the row. The Conversation Content Panel opens inline with the full exchange in chronological order. If the user uploaded a file during the session, it appears as a downloadable link.
  4. To archive the conversation, select the row and click Download Conversations. The system produces a timestamped ZIP with one folder containing a JSON metadata file and all uploaded files. The Message Log confirms the result; the Application Monitor records it under the Joule Conversation Download run type.
  5. To remove the conversation after archiving, select it and choose Delete. Confirm in the dialog. The conversation, its messages, and its files are gone.
  6. Open the Application Monitor via Menu > System > Application Monitor. The deletion log entry is there under the Joule Conversation Deletion run type, with the Conversation ID. That record stays even after the conversation is deleted.

 

From start to finish: the conversation was created by a team member, reviewed by an administrator, exported as a ZIP, deleted from the active list, and its audit entry confirmed in the Application Monitor.

 

Wrapping Up

 

Compliance teams are asking for a record of AI interactions. A manager wanting to know why Joule gave a particular answer last Tuesday. A periodic cleanup of conversations that no longer need to be in the system. These are the situations the AI Conversation Monitor is built for, and it handles all of them from a single screen in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model.

 

How are you using it? Focused on compliance tracking, investigating specific AI responses, or managing conversation volume over time? Share your approach in the comments.

 

I hope this post gives you a solid picture of what the AI Conversation Monitor can do. If you have questions, reach out via the SAP Profitability and Performance Management Community.

 

Related Resources

  • AI Conversation Monitor on the SAP Help Portal. Official documentation covering screen layout, available actions, role prerequisites, and step-by-step procedure.

entry.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model What’s New as of 2026-09-07
entry.content:
Hello SAP Community, 

We're thrilled to share another round of updates for SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud – Universal Model (SAP PaPM Cloud UM).

This release brings a range of enhancements designed to simplify tasks, improve productivity, and give you greater control over your business processes.

Read on to discover the latest features, see what's changed, and learn how you can make the most of these new capabilities.

Happy reading!

 

JOULE IN UNIVERSAL MODEL

 

OCR-Based Image Processing Support in Joule 

Joule's file processing capabilities expand further with the introduction of Optical Character Recognition. Users can now upload documents containing images, charts, diagrams, and visuals from any screen in SAP Profitability and Performance Cloud Universal Model (SAP PaPM Cloud UM), and Joule will extract and interpret the content, enabling richer, more accurate answers from complex, image-heavy files. 

Image Processing via File Upload 

Users can upload files containing embedded images from any screen in SAP PaPM Cloud UM. Joule processes the visual content using OCR (Optical Character Recognition) and extracts information from a wide range of content types: 

  • Charts: bar charts (data values), line charts (trends), pie charts (percentages) 
  • Tables: structured data with rows and columns 
  • Diagrams: flowcharts (steps and decisions), org charts (hierarchy) 
  • Text images: scanned documents and memos 
  • Photos: images with visible text 
  • Mixed content: infographics and dashboards containing a combination of text, images, charts, and diagrams 

 

 

 

 

Image Processor Toggle in Joule Settings 

Users and administrators can control whether OCR image processing is active through the Joule Settings panel. 

  • Navigate to Joule Settings and enable or disable the Image Processor toggle. 
  • When disabled, Joule will not process embedded image content from uploaded files. 
  • This toggle allows users to manage their token usage effectively. 

 

OCR Activation Requirements 

OCR image processing is effective only when both of the following conditions are met simultaneously: 

  • The tenant destination is configured with an ocr_model parameter within the PAPM_UM_AI_UNIVERSAL destination. 
  • The Image Processor toggle is enabled in the Joule Settings in the UI. 

 

Note: OCR is available for intensive Joule usage only. It is not active for light (no-destination) usage. 

Recommended OCR Models 

Two models are supported for OCR processing: 

  • gemini-3.1-flash-lite - primary model for OCR (more cost-effective) 
  • gemini-2.5-flash - alternative model for OCR (for regions where the primary model is not supported) 

Summary 

With OCR support, Joule can now handle documents that go beyond plain text - extracting insights from charts, diagrams, visuals, and scanned content embedded in uploaded files. The feature supports complex, mixed documents containing a combination of text and visual elements. Combined with the flexible Image Processor toggle, users have greater control over how Joule processes file content, making it easier to work with data-rich documents across all screens in PaPM UM. 

More details are available in the SAP Help Portal under Create SAP BTP Cockpit HTTP Destination in Universal Model and Using Joule in Universal Model. 

 

 

MODEL

 

Manage Connections: Access to Model Views in AddOn Environment Connection 

SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model continue to enhance flexibility and model governance across environments. Following the innovation announced in SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model What’s New as of 2026-06-01, users can now access Model Views through connections configured with the “AddOn Environment” connection type. 

This enhancement represents an important step forward in simplifying model reuse and strengthening consistency across environments. It expands the capabilities of “AddOn Environment” connections by enabling seamless integration of both Model Entities and Model Views, providing users with greater visibility and broader modeling options while maintaining centralized governance. 

What’s New? 

Previously, as described in Connections in PaPM Cloud Universal Model and SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model: What’s New as of 2025.09.01?, “AddOn Environment” connections supported only Model Entities from the target environment. 

With this latest enhancement, “AddOn Environment” connections now support: 

  • Active Model Entities 
  • Active Model Views 
  • Adoption of target environment data controls 
  • Inheritance of master data associations 

All functions with an API State = “Active” are made available through the connection, allowing organizations to leverage a more complete and governed representation of the target model. 

For additional information regarding API State management, refer to Change API State of Function in the Application Help for Universal Model. 

 

How It Works 

When creating a new connection and selecting “AddOn Environment” as the connection type, users now have the option to enable the checkbox Target Model Views. 

Once selected, the connection will retrieve and display all active Model Views together with all active Model Entities from the target environment. This provides a unified and comprehensive view of the available model objects that can be referenced. 

An additional improvement of usability allows users to easily identify the Original Type of each synchronized function, clearly distinguishing between Model Views and Model Entities. This improves transparency and helps users better understand the source and nature of the synchronized objects. 

If the Target Model Views checkbox is not selected, the behavior remains unchanged, and only active Model Entities are displayed. 

Consistent Model Governance Across Environments 

One of the key strengths of the “AddOn Environment” connection type is its focus on consistency and governance. Using this connection, users can reference and reuse the configurations of Model Entities and Model Views, including: 

  • Dataset definitions 
  • Data controls 
  • Association fields 

These components are transferred and consumed through the Model Reference function, making it easier to establish standardized models across multiple environments. 

To preserve alignment with the source environment, the Target Model Views checkbox accessed through an “AddOn Environment” connection remains read-only after the connection has been created. This behavior applies regardless of whether the Target Model Views option was enabled during connection setup.  

This design ensures that the structure defined in the target environment is maintained exactly as intended. Field definitions, configurations, and function structures cannot be modified in the consuming environment, maintaining a consistent data model across environments. 

By extending “AddOn Environment” support beyond Model Entities, SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model provides users with an even more powerful framework for managing enterprise-wide data models while preserving the integrity of centrally defined structures. 

For further details, see Manage Connections – AddOn Environment in the Application Help for Universal Model.  

 

 

Call OData endpoints with Parameter Model Using the Reader Function 

We are excited to introduce an enhancement to the Reader function that simplifies the consumption of parameterized “OData Services” connections. 

With this update, the Reader now fully supports retrieving data from OData endpoints that require parameters, using a Parameter Model in combination with a Function Model. 

When an “OData Service” connection contains a Function Model with an associated Parameter Model, the Reader automatically identifies and utilizes the required parameters at runtime.

Since the Reader function is designed to accept only a single input, users don’t need to explicitly provide the Parameter Model. Once the connection metadata is synchronized, the system automatically detects the relevant Parameter Model through the OData function definition and applies it during run. 

Important Prerequisite 

Before using OData functions in the Reader, verify that any Parameter Model association with a Function Model is synchronized and active in the Models section of the “OData Service Connection”.  

If a required Parameter Model is Inactive or Not Synchronized, the Reader will not be able to run the function successfully, and an error will be shown in the Event Logs indicating that the required function is not active. 

Key Behaviors 

  • Parameter Model synchronized but no data in Parameter Model:  
    1. Foreground run: Running the Function Model in foreground displays an error when Parameter Model contains no data;  
     
    2. Background run: Running the Function Model in background completes with zero records and adds an informative message in Event Logs indicating that Parameter Model requires Data records.

  • Parameter Model synchronized with valid data: The Reader runs successfully and returns the expected data.

Results and record count can be verified in Event Logs.

Stay tuned for more information on this topic in an upcoming technical blog post. 

 

REPORT SCREEN

 

Manual Refresh and Recent Changes in Reports 

Reports now include a manual refresh capability along with a Recent Changes indicator that notifies you when underlying data or report configuration has been updated. This gives you direct control over when report content is refreshed and provides visibility into what changed. 

What's New 

A Recent Changes icon is now available in the report header. Choosing this icon displays the last five event log entries and a Refresh button that refreshes all page elements on the current page. 

When Auto-refresh is turned off, a notification banner appears automatically when a change is detected in any function within the report environment — including data updates, creations, or deletions — or when the report configuration itself is modified. The banner provides two options: 

  • Refresh Outdated – Refreshes only the page elements on the current page that are affected by the detected changes. 
  • Refresh All – Refreshes all page elements on the current page.

When Auto-refresh is turned on, outdated elements are refreshed automatically, and the banner is not displayed. 

Each page element's toolbar also now includes an individual Refresh icon, allowing you to refresh a specific element independently. 

The Data screen also supports this enhancement: a notification banner appears when the function has been changed by another user, prompting you to refresh the screen with the latest data. 

 

 

DATA SCREEN

 

Priority Value in Pivot Mode

When analyzing data, the most important information should be visible immediately. With the new Priority Value setting in Pivot Mode, SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model gives you greater control over how pivot columns are displayed, helping you bring key values to the forefront of your analysis.

Whether you're working on the Data screen or using Insert Show Element in a report, you can now define a specific value that should appear first within a pivot column group. This makes it easier to focus on critical data without manually searching through multiple columns.

Example

Imagine you're analyzing regional sales data and want to review “Europe” first every time the report is displayed. By setting “Europe” as the Priority Value, the corresponding pivot column is automatically shown before the other regions, providing faster access to the data that is most relevant to your analysis.

Why Use Priority Value?

Pivot tables often generate a large number of columns, making it difficult to quickly locate the values that matter most. By assigning a Priority Value, you can:

  • Prioritize key business-relevant values
  • Improve report readability and usability
  • Focus attention on important categories or dimensions
  • Create a more consistent analytical view across reports

How It Works

When a value is specified as a Priority Value, its corresponding pivot column is displayed first within the Column Labels group, followed by the remaining columns.

How to Use It

  1. On the Data screen or within Insert Show Element on the Report screen, choose Columns and activate Pivot Mode.
  2. Drag the field that you want to use as column headers to the Column Labels section.
  3. Choose Settings beside the field name.
  4. In the Priority Value field, enter the value that should appear first within the column group.

After you save your settings, the pivot column for the specified value is displayed before the other columns in the same group, making important information easier to identify and analyze.

 

Multi-Select Priority Value for Pivot Column Label Sorting

When working in Pivot Mode, you can now specify multiple priority values for sorting combination columns within Column Labels. This gives you greater flexibility when applying multiple filters and working with alternate priority columns. 

What's New 

The Priority Value field in the Column Labels sorting settings now supports multiple values, enabling you to define more precise sorting combinations. Multiple values are separated by a semicolon (;). This applies to fields backed by master data as well as other input field types. When multiple filters are active and create multiple combination columns, each combination column is sorted according to its corresponding priority value in the defined sequence. 

 

Control Column Visibility in Pivot Mode

You can now define which value columns are displayed in pivot mode within the Data screen and Report screen (Show Element). The new Hidden Conditions feature gives you precise control over column visibility based on column label combinations, helping you focus on the data that matters most. 

When Pivot Mode is enabled, a Hidden Conditions icon button appears on each item in the Values section. Choose this icon to open the Hidden Conditions dialog for that specific value. In this dialog, you define rules that determine when a column should be hidden based on its label combination. 

The dialog provides two condition sections: 

  • Including — Columns whose labels match the conditions defined here are hidden from the pivot grid. 
  • Excluding — Columns matching these conditions remain visible, even if they also match an Including condition. Excluding conditions always take priority. 

Within a single condition, you can stack multiple AND filter rows to narrow the match. Across separate condition objects, conditions are evaluated as OR. This flexible structure lets you tailor column visibility to fit complex layout requirements. 

Hidden condition settings are saved as part of the layout. When you save a layout or switch between layout variants, the configured visibility rules are preserved and applied automatically. Your pivot view remains consistent each time you open or return to the same layout. 

 For more information, see Pivot Mode

 

Support Multiple Value Helps

This release introduces a connected set of enhancements that work together to provide hierarchy-based value selection in the Dynamic Rule Screen. You can now define hierarchy structures using the new Master Data Key and Parent Key value help tags in Model Entity and Model View - Projection, assign them through the Hierarchy Data Function on Association fields, and use the new Open List dialog to browse and select fields, master data values, and hierarchy values directly when creating rules. Together, these enhancements simplify configuration, improve data consistency, and provide a more intuitive value selection experience across SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model.

How the Feature Works Together

Model Entity / Model View
(Parent Key + Master Data Key)

Association Field
(Hierarchy Data Function)

Dynamic Rule Screen
(Open List with Hierarchy Selection)

Define the Hierarchy Structure in Model Entity and Model View

Consider a scenario where your model tracks intercompany transactions across a group of legal entities. For example, EMEA contains Germany, France, and Spain, which in turn contain individual business units. This parent-child relationship exists in your data, but without the right configuration, the system cannot expose it as a hierarchical tree in the value selection dialog.

To make the hierarchy visible and usable, you assign two new Value Help Tags to the relevant fields in a Model Entity or Model View – Projection function.

Value Help Tags

  • Parent Key: Specifies the field that identifies the parent record in the hierarchy. This field establishes the parent-child relationship used to build the hierarchical tree. The field tagged as Parent Key must reference another record within the same function (a self-reference).
  • Master Data Key: Specifies the field that represents the master data value in the hierarchy. Use this tag when the hierarchy key differs from the master data value — for example, when hierarchy nodes are used as grouping containers and a separate field holds the actual business value.

These tags work alongside the existing Key tag to give the system the full picture of the hierarchy:

  • Key: Unique node identifier.
  • Parent Key: Parent-child relationship.
  • Master Data Key: Displays business value.

In Model Entity


Note: The field tagged as Parent Key must reference another record within the same Model Entity to establish the hierarchy relationship.
For more information, see Configure Simple Model Entity.

In Model View - Projection

The same Parent Key and Master Data Key tags are also available in Model View – Projection functions. This means you can define the hierarchy structure over a projected view rather than a base entity — useful when you want to apply column or row pruning before exposing the hierarchy.

Note: All fields assigned hierarchy Value Help Tag must be included in the projection output. This ensures the hierarchy displays correctly.
For more information, see Model View – Projection

Assign the Hierarchy Data Function to Association Fields

With the hierarchy defined in a Model Entity or Model View - Projection, the next step is connecting it to the field that interact with the Association field.

An Association field already has a Master Data Function that provides the list of valid business values for selection. Think of the Master Data Function as answering the question: *what values can be selected?* The new Hierarchy Data Function answers a different question: *how are those values organized?*  It points to the Model Entity or Model View - Projection you configured in the previous step and allows the master data values to be displayed into a hierarchical tree.

After activation, the Association field is hierarchy-enabled and ready to surface the value selection dialog in supported screens.
For more information, see Manage Fields - Association.

Use Hierarchies with the Open List in the Data Screen and Dynamic Rule Screen

With the hierarchy structure defined and the Hierarchy Data Function assigned, the Open List icon appears on the Association field in the Data Screen and Dynamic Rule Screen. You can select this icon directly from conditions, assignments, and filters to open a structured value selection dialog.

The dialog provides up to three tabs, depending on the field configuration.

  • Fields - Field paths from the function.
  • Master Data - Master data reference value.
  • Hierarchy - Hierarchical values organized in parent-child relationships, built from the configured Hierarchy Data Function.

Note: The feature is available for Flow function and Model Flow function.

For more information, see Dynamic Rules Screen.

 

CALCULATION

 

Enhanced Formula Editing in Calculation Function 

The Calculation function now supports an enhanced formula editor for writing and editing formulas in the Assignments section. This brings syntax highlighting and an expanded editing area to formula authoring, making it easier to write and validate complex HANA Cloud expressions — consistent with the experience already available in the Model Calculation function. 

What's New 

When a Calculation function rule is in Edit mode, an Edit button is now available in the Formula column of the Assignments section. Choosing the Edit button opens the Edit Formula dialog, which displays an expanded formula editing area with syntax highlighting. The editor pre-populates with the existing formula value if one has already been saved or starts empty for new formulas. 

 

FLOW AND MODEL FLOW

A new way to transfer transform data. Both let you apply rule-based logic to your data — but each serves a different purpose, and together they cover a wide range of business scenarios. 

What's New

Flow: Turn Input Data into Postings 

The Flow function is designed for scenarios where you need to transform input records and optionally store the results into a result model function. You define rules that filter your data, apply conditions, and assign output values — then Flow writes the processed results directly to a target model entity. 

It is a good fit for use cases like generating financial postings, applying value adjustments based on business logic, or running large-scale rule imports using dynamic rules from a CSV file. 

Model Flow: Analyze Without Writing 

The Model Flow function uses the same rule configuration as Flow, but instead of writing results to a target, it exposes the transformed output as a read-only analytical view. No data is stored — The results are available directly for reporting and simulation. 

This makes it ideal for previewing rule results, building reports on top of calculated data, or testing your logic before committing using a write-back scenario. 

Which One Should You Use? 

  • Need to store results and feed them into downstream processes? → Flow 
  • Need to analyze or simulate rule results without persisting data? → Model Flow 

Both functions are available in Universal Model and share the same configuration experience, so switching between them is straightforward once you know what your use case requires. 

For the full configuration, see the following guides:  

  • Flow 
  • Model Flow 
  • Meet Flow and Model Flow: New Rule-Based Posting Functions in SAP PaPM Universal Model

entry.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: What's New as of 2026-09-07?
entry.content:
Hello, SAP Community! 👋

Welcome back to another What’s New in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model!

For this release, the spotlight is on Joule . Looking at the enhancements together, I realized that a screen-by-screen tour would not quite tell the whole story.

This time, let’s take a different approach. Some enhancements change how you talk to Joule, while others give you more context when you manage and monitor Joule. 🔎

So, What's New?

The enhancements in this release are related to the following areas:

Talk to Joule

Personalize new conversations and make your intent clearer from the start.

Enhancement

What's New

Your Joule Rules

Save personal preferences for new conversations.

Ask or Act

Choose whether Joule shall answer a question or perform a supported action.

 Manage and Monitor Joule

Get more context when reviewing logged events, conversations, and configuration changes.

Enhancement

What's New

Conversation ID and Performed By

Identify the Joule conversation associated with an action, and determine whether the action originated from Joule, a user, or the system.

Download and Upload

Export and restore Joule conversation archives.

Settings Update

Review changes made to Joule AI Settings.


Let’s start with the enhancements you’ll encounter while working directly with Joule.

Talk to Joule

Your Joule Rules: Save the Instructions You Keep Repeating

Previously, Joule responded to each conversation using its built-in system instructions. If you wanted Joule to consistently consider personal preferences, such as a specific response language, preferred format, or level of detail, you had to specify those preferences again when starting a new conversation.

With Your Joule Rules, you can save personal instructions that Joule considers as additional context when you start a new conversation.

You can define up to 1,000 characters of personal instructions. Rules are saved per user and persist across all environments and sessions.

For example: Respond in English. Put the conclusion first. Use concise tables for comparisons.

This lets you use your saved instructions for general response preferences while keeping your prompts focused on the specific task.

How to Configure Your Joule Rules

  1. Open Joule in Report Management.
  2. Open the side navigation panel, choose Settings.
  3. Enter your instructions in Your Joule Rules.
  4. Save the settings.
  5. Start a new conversation.

Your Joule Rules settings

Your Joule Rules applied to a new conversation

Important: Your Joule Rules is optional. If you leave the field empty, Joule continues to respond without additional personal instructions.

Here are a few additional details worth keeping in mind:

  • Changes apply to new conversations only.
  • Existing conversations are not affected.
  • Content that conflicts with security policies or internal Joule guidelines can be ignored.
  • No specific feedback is shown when a rule is filtered.
  • The system does not guarantee that every rule will be applied in every response.

For more information, see Manage Joule Conversations.

Ask or Act: Choose How You Want Joule to Respond

Sometimes you want Joule to answer a question. Other times, you want Joule to perform an action.

Joule in Report Management now includes an Ask or Act toggle above the message input field.

Ask or Act toggle in Joule – Report Management

Ask

Choose Ask when you want Joule to provide information, such as an explanation, summary, comparison, or another read-only response.

For example:

  • Summarize the key findings in this report.
  • Which region has the highest revenue?

Act

Choose Act when you want Joule to perform a supported action on your behalf.

For example: Create a bar chart using the revenue measure by region.

For more information, see:

  • Joule in Report Management
  • SAP Business AI (Joule) Setup

For additional background on Joule capabilities in Report Management, see SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: Joule AI – Features and Capabilities in Report Management.

Manage and Monitor Joule

Talking to Joule is only one side of the picture. Sometimes, you also need to look beyond the conversation itself to understand how an action was performed, identify its associated conversation, retain conversation records, or review changes to Joule AI settings.

That’s where the next enhancements come in.

Conversation ID and Performed By: More Context in the Monitors

When Joule performs an action, the new monitoring information helps you understand how the action was performed and identify the associated conversation.

The Application Monitor, Process Monitor, and History Monitor already provide records of system events, including timestamps and statuses.

With Joule able to initiate supported actions, knowing that an action occurred is only part of the picture. You may also need to understand where that action came from.

Two new read-only columns provide that context:

  • Conversation ID

This contains the unique identifier of the associated Joule conversation.

You can use this ID to identify the Joule conversation associated with the monitor entry.

For example, if you are investigating a report change and find a monitor entry where Performed By is Joule, you can use the associated Conversation ID to identify the related Joule conversation.

  • Performed By

This helps you distinguish whether an action was performed directly by a user, initiated through Joule, or performed by an automated system process.

Value

Meaning

Joule

The action was initiated by a user through Joule and carried out by Joule.

System

The action was performed by an automated system process.

User

The action was performed directly by a user.

When reviewing monitor entries, you can now identify whether an event originated from a user, Joule, or the system.

Application Monitor

Conversation ID and Performed By in the Application Monitor

Process Monitor

Conversation ID and Performed By in the Process Monitor

History Monitor

Conversation ID and Performed By in the History Monitor

Important: For monitor entries created before this enhancement, Performed By and Conversation ID are blank.

A few additional details are worth keeping in mind:

  • Conversation ID is populated only for Joule-initiated entries.
  • It remains blank for User and System entries.
  • Both columns support sorting and filtering.
  • The system value for Performed By is currently used by the Process Scheduler.
  • System entries are currently visible in the Application Monitor and Process Monitor, but not in the History Monitor.

For more information, see:

  • Application Monitor
  • Process Monitor
  • History Monitor

Download and Upload: Export and Restore Conversations

Sometimes, you need to review or retain the conversation itself. The AI Conversation Monitor now supports downloading and uploading Joule conversations.

Administrators can select one or more conversations and download them as a timestamped ZIP archive.

Downloading conversations from the AI Conversation Monitor

A previously downloaded archive can also be uploaded to restore the conversations to the system.

Uploading conversations to the AI Conversation Monitor

With the required administrative access, downloading conversations gives you another way to retain conversation records for offline review, troubleshooting, quality assurance, or an organization’s approved archival process.

Uploading a previously downloaded archive allows those conversations to be restored when needed.

Note: Joule is powered by generative AI. Review its output before use.

System administrators can access conversations for security, troubleshooting, quality assurance, and applicable governance purposes. Do not enter sensitive personal data or other personal data that you do not want to be processed.

For more information, see Joule Data Protection and Privacy.

For a detailed walkthrough of the AI Conversation Monitor, including access roles, archive contents, and an end-to-end archival scenario, see SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model – Introducing the AI Conversation Monitor.

Settings Update: Review What Changed in Joule AI Settings

The last enhancement takes us away from conversations and into configuration.

Knowing how Joule is configured is useful. But when you are investigating unexpected behavior, another question can be just as important: What has changed?

Changes made to Joule AI Settings are now logged using a dedicated run type: Settings Update.

These entries are available in the Application Monitor, Process Monitor, and the message logs on the Settings screen.

Logging applies when a user sets, changes, or clears values for settings such as:

  • Default SAP AI Core Destination Name
  • Default AI Model
  • Reasoning AI Model
  • Web Search Model

Changes to Web Search, including activating or deactivating the feature, are also logged.

When a setting is changed, the log provides information about the previous and new values.

Settings Update logs for changes to Joule AI Settings

For more information about run types, see Event Status and Run Types.

Before We Go…

There’s always more to discover with Joule, and we hope these enhancements improve your day-to-day experience.

Which enhancement are you most looking forward to?

Drop your favorite enhancement in the comments. 💬

Ciao for now! 👋

entry.title: Choosing the Right BYOD Database Option for SAP PaPM Cloud in SAP Business Data Cloud
entry.content:
When deploying SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud (SAP PaPM Cloud) with the Bring Your Own Database (BYOD) approach in SAP Business Data Cloud, one of the key architecture decisions is whether to use SAP Datasphere or a dedicated SAP HANA Cloud instance.

Both options are based on SAP HANA technology, but they are suited to different types of uses cases and workloads.

In practice,

  • SAP Datasphere in BDC is the perfect fit for Seamless Planning and moderate data volume scenarios,
  • while a dedicated SAP HANA Cloud instance in BDC is the best choice when PaPM workloads become larger or more resource intensive.

SAP PaPM Cloud with SAP Datasphere

SAP Datasphere is especially relevant when it is already part of the customer’s planning and data architecture.

A typical example is Seamless Planning, where SAP Analytics Cloud, SAP Datasphere, and SAP PaPM Cloud are used together in an integrated scenario.

For these use cases, and for workloads in the range of a few million records, SAP Datasphere is the best BYOD option. Record count alone, however, does not determine the actual workload. Model complexity, joins, allocations, and parallel processing also play an important role.

Why Workload Size Matters

SAP Datasphere is a managed service and therefore applies workload management to protect the stability of the overall environment.

This is usually transparent to the application, but it becomes more relevant for PaPM scenarios that generate heavy database processing.

Large allocations, complex calculations, high data volumes, or several processes running in parallel can consume significant database resources. In these situations, workload limits can be reached and individual statements may be restricted or rejected by the workload management layer.

For smaller and moderate workloads, this is typically not an issue. For larger workload scenarios, however, it should be considered during the architecture design.

SAP PaPM Cloud with Dedicated SAP HANA Cloud

For high volume or compute intensive SAP PaPM Cloud workloads, we recommend using a dedicated SAP HANA Cloud instance in the BDC Formation as the BYOD option.

The main advantage is that the HANA Cloud instance is used exclusively for the high SAP PaPM Cloud workload. This gives more control over sizing and allows the database resources to be aligned with the expected processing requirements.

This is particularly relevant when the scenario involves large datasets, complex calculation chains, high concurrency, or intensive parallel processing.

The dedicated HANA Cloud instance can still be part of the overall SAP Business Data Cloud landscape. Customers can therefore keep the benefits of BDC (for instance to consume BDC Data Products in SAP PaPM Cloud) while using a database environment that is better suited to demanding SAP PaPM Cloud processing.

Architecture Guidance

Scenario

Recommended BYOD Option

Seamless Planning

SAP Datasphere

Moderate volume planning workloads

SAP Datasphere

High volume production processing

Dedicated SAP HANA Cloud

Resource intensive calculations

Dedicated SAP HANA Cloud

High concurrency or parallel processing

Dedicated SAP HANA Cloud


Conclusion

The decision should mainly be driven by the expected workload.

For integrated planning scenarios and moderate processing volumes, SAP Datasphere is the best fit.

For larger and more resource intensive PaPM workloads, a dedicated SAP HANA Cloud instance is the recommended option.

Considering this early in the project helps avoid performance constraints later and gives customers a clearer path as their SAP PaPM Cloud models and data volumes grow. Until next time!

entry.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: Notification Management in User Preferences
entry.content:
Hello Everyone! 

This blog post introduces the enhanced Notifications section under User Preferences in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model (SAP PaPM Cloud SM). This feature allows you to configure your notification preferences by selecting which notification types you receive and for which environments, resulting in a more focused and relevant notification experience.  

Note 

This feature is dependent on the notifications configuration performed by system administrators on a global level via Settings → Global Notification Settings. 

To learn more, please see the links below: 

  • SAP Help Portal – User Preferences in Standard Model
  • SAP Help Portal – Global Notification Settings in Standard Model

Notification Management Overview 

Navigation path: User Profile → User Preferences → Notifications 

The Notifications tab replaces the previous notification settings in User Preferences and introduces two dedicated sub-tabs: 

  • Notification Types – Allows you to configure the types of notifications you want to receive, and the delivery channels through which they are sent.
  • Environments – Allows you to specify the environments for which you receive notifications. 

Notification Types Tab 

The Notification Types tab displays a table listing all available notification categories. Each row represents a notification type, while each column corresponds to a delivery channel. You can independently activate or deactivate each notification type for each available delivery channel. 

The following notification types are available for configuration: 

  • Activity changes 
  • Private environment changes 
  • Process changes 
  • Scheduled jobs 
  • Team changes 

For example, you can choose to receive Activity changes notifications through the in-app channel only, while keeping multiple delivery channels enabled for Scheduled jobs notifications. This level of granularity ensures that you receive updates through the channels that best suit your workflow and preferences.

How Global Notification Settings Affect User Preferences 

Some in-app or email notification types cannot be activated or deactivated by users because they are configured by an administrator at the system level. 

For further details on how administrators configure at system level, refer to the SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model: Global Notification Settings. 

Example: 

Let's assume that your administrator has configured the global notification settings as follows: 

  • Activity changes → Always send 
  • Private environment changes → Always send 
  • Process changes → Allow users to manage settings 
  • Scheduled jobs → Allow users to manage settings 
  • Team changes → Never send 

In this scenario, the only notification categories that you can configure in User Preferences → Notifications are Process changes and Scheduled jobs. The settings for all other notification categories are managed centrally by your administrator and cannot be changed by individual users.

Environments Tab 

The Environments tab allows you to define the scope of environments for which notifications are generated. The following options are available: 

  • All environments – You receive notifications for changes that occur in all environments to which you have access. 
  • Select environments – You can choose the specific environments for which you want to receive notifications. 
  • All environments with the exception of – You receive notifications for changes that occur in all accessible environments, except those that you explicitly exclude. 

When you select Select environments or All environments except, use the search field and the scrollable list of environments to specify the environments to include or exclude from notifications. 

I hope this article has provided a clear overview of the Notifications section and how it can be used to create a more relevant and efficient notification experience in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model. 

Please stay tuned for the next blog post! 🔔

entry.title: Prompting Techniques for Joule in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model
entry.content:
For years, finance teams have faced the same challenge: good ideas sitting in backlogs, waiting on development schedules and stretched IT resources. An allocation model, a profitability view, a transfer pricing scenario - turning a business need into a working solution has always taken longer than it should.

With Joule, that changes. Finance leaders describe what they need in plain language, and Joule turns that intent into a live model - drawing on existing environments as design blueprints, policy documents for the rules, and the specifics of the conversation for everything else. What once took weeks of back-and-forth between finance and IT can now start taking shape in a single session.

Let's see a practical example of how a requirement turns into a working SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model (SAP PaPM): NovaSpark is a boutique marketing agency with three major clients - “TechFlow” (€420k), “RetailCo” (€310k), and “GreenBrand” (€180k). On paper, all profitable. But salaries, office rent, software subscriptions, and management overhead all sit in a single unallocated block. Nobody actually knows which client is making money and which one is being subsidized.

The CFO knew the answer lived in a cost allocation model. What she didn't have was three days to build one. What she had was Joule.

This post walks through the entire build - from scratch to a working allocation model (a fully configured SAP PaPM UM environment, ready to run - using nothing but Joule prompts. Every prompt is real, every response is what you'd see in the chat panel, and every step shows which capability is doing the work.

The Anatomy of a SAP Profitablitiy and Performance Management Build

Every SAP PaPM UM Cloud model follows the similar sequence - regardless of complexity:

  1. Create an Environment : the container for all fields, functions, and data
  2. Define Fields : dimensions (Account, Customer, Activity) and measures (Amount) that structure the model
  3. Configure Allocation Functions : define sender/receiver logic and the driver basis for each cost flow stage
  4. Activate the Environment : deploy to runtime so data can be loaded and functions can run
  5. Load Master Data : populate dimension reference tables before any transactional data can reference them
  6. Load Source Data : load GL postings, driver percentages, and headcount figures into Manual Entry functions
  7. Run the Allocation Chain : run functions in sequence; output flows into downstream stages
  8. Build Reports : create KPIs and profitability views on top of allocation output

Each step traditionally means multiple configuration screens. In this walkthrough, every one happens through a Joule prompt.

Before We Build Anything: Ask First
