Before you start building anything in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Universal Model Cloud, here’s a quick habit that’ll save you a ton of time, spend five minutes in Ask mode - Joule's inquiry mode where you can ask questions to understand how Profitability and Performance Management operates.

For NovaSpark, the first question is simple: does anything useful already exist?

"Show me all active environments in PaPM and list any that relate to cost allocation or profitability."

Joule comes back with all 12 active environments, flags SXP2409 and RESTPROFIT as the two relevant to cost allocation and profitability, and immediately offers to explore either one. Every environment name is a live citation link - hover to preview, click to navigate.

SXP2409 is the closest match. A quick follow-up scopes straight into it: Then, using the @mention scoping feature, you can drill straight into that environment:

“@SXP2409 @RESTPROFIT What fields are defined here? Can any be used for a new client profitability model?”

RESTPROFIT has 6 fields - a basic P&L structure. SXP2409 has 65, covering dimensions, allocation drivers, amounts, and hierarchy fields. The key takeaway: fields are environment-specific in PaPM, so nothing carries across directly. But SXP2409's design is a ready-made blueprint - Customer, AmountInLocalCurrency, ActivityDriver, ResourceDriver, Scenario, Period, FiscalYear are all directly applicable. Joule flags three additions worth making for NovaSpark's use case: Client Segment, Service Line, and Allocated Overhead.

Five minutes in, you have a field design for NOVA2024 grounded in a proven model structure, not guesswork.

One more question before touching the configuration for real:

"What is the difference between a View function and an Allocation function in PaPM? When should I use each one?"

This is Application Help - Joule's ability to answer "how does SAP PaPM UM Cloud actually work" questions in context, with links to its own documentation. You get a clear explanation: a View function filters and cleans data without modifying the source; an Allocation function moves costs between objects using driver-based rules. For NovaSpark, the answer is one View function to clean the raw data, then three Allocation functions to stage the cost flow. The SAP PaPM help link is right there if you want to go deeper.

Ask mode carries no risk. You can't break anything in it. And the five minutes you spend here means the next two hours go faster because you're not discovering structural constraints mid-build.

Creating the Environment

When you're ready to actually build something, you're in Act mode - and Act mode is where configuration actually happens. That's exactly why Joule includes an approval flow for every sensitive operation.

"Create a new environment called 'NovaSpark 2024 Client Profitability' with ID NOVA2024. It will be used for overhead cost allocation and client profitability analysis for fiscal year 2024."

Before anything runs, Joule pauses and shows you exactly what it's about to do:

The environment is created, and the response includes a live citation link to it in PaPM. One prompt. The container exists.

Defining the Fields

Fields are the dimensions and measures your model is built on - the columns that give raw data meaning. The SXP2409 exploration gave a clear blueprint: Account, Customer, AmountInLocalCurrency, Activity, Resource, ActivityDriver, ResourceDriver, Scenario, Period, FiscalYear, CostCenter. NOVA2024 gets its own set modelled on that proven structure, extended with the three NovaSpark-specific fields Joule flagged - ClientSegment, ServiceLine, and AllocatedOverhead.

The prompting technique here is batching. Don't send individual prompts for each field. Describe the full set in one go:

"Create the following fields in the NOVA2024 environment based on our client profitability model design:

  • Account - string, GL account code, key field
  • Customer - string, client identifier (TechFlow, RetailCo, GreenBrand)
  • CostCenter - string, internal department or team
  • Activity - string, service activity (Strategy, Creative, Operations, BusinessDevelopment)
  • Resource - string, resource pool (SalaryResource, FacilitiesResource, TechnologyResource, ManagementResource)
  • ActivityDriver - string, basis for activity allocation
  • ResourceDriver - string, basis for resource allocation
  • Scenario - string, ACT for actuals
  • FiscalYear - string, fiscal year
  • Period - string, accounting period 1–12
  • AmountInLocalCurrency - decimal, amount in EUR
  • Adjustment - decimal, percentage-based allocation driver
  • ClientSegment - string, client tier or industry grouping (new - specific to NovaSpark)
  • ServiceLine - string, revenue category by service type (new)
  • *AllocatedOverhead - decimal, indirect cost amount post-allocation (new)”

Checking the Allocation Policy (Before Configuring Logic)

Here's where Joule's Attach File capability earns its place in a real build.

NovaSpark's finance director wrote an overhead allocation policy document two years ago. Before configuring any allocation logic, the CFO wants to make sure the model follows it. She attaches "NovaSpark_Overhead_Policy_2022.pdf" via the paperclip icon in the chat panel and asks:

"Read this policy document and tell me whether our planned allocation approach - salary accounts to resource pools, then to activities, then to clients - is consistent with what it specifies."

Joule reads the PDF, cross-references it against the model design described in the conversation, and returns a structured policy alignment assessment - three gaps flagged, each with the exact policy section as the source.

Three different configurations, caught before a single function was configured. All three would have required rework if discovered post-build.

"Yes — build based on the policy specifications."

Multi-turn context carries all three constraints forward automatically into every subsequent step. No need to repeat them.

Benchmarking the Allocation Percentages (Web Search)

Before finalising the time-based allocation percentages, the CFO wants an external sanity check. The planned salary split is: Strategy 60%, Creative 30%, Operations 10%.

"What's the typical overhead allocation split between strategy, creative, and operations in boutique marketing agencies? Are our planned percentages reasonable?"

Web Search pulls current industry benchmarks and runs a pool-by-pool assessment. (See screenshot.) The verdict: reasonable and defensible - with two watch points. Operations salary at 10% is lean against an industry norm of 15–20%, and the Facilities 0% to Creative needs validating against actual headcount. Both are adjustable at any time by updating the Resource Pool to Activity Percentage Splits driver table - no function changes required.

Building the Function Model

That single confirmation - "Yes - build based on the policy specifications" - was the build instruction. Joule structured and created the entire allocation model from it.

Three stages, 12 master data functions, three driver tables - all following the policy exactly:

  • Stage 1: Stage 1: GL Accounts to Resource Pools - holds overhead GL postings tagged by resource pool
  • Stage 2: Four allocation functions - Salary (PER, 35/50/10/5), Facilities (FCT, headcount per §3.4), Technology (PER, 70/20/10), Management (PER, 40/20/20/20) - each reading from Resource Pool to Activity Percentage Splits or FTE Headcount by Activity (Facilities Driver)
  • Stage 3: Stage 3: Activities to Client Engagements (Time-Tracking) - reads from Time-Tracking Activity to Client Percentages, offset mapping Service Activity → Customer

The model structure is fully configured. The policy constraints - four pools, headcount for Facilities, four activity codes - were applied automatically throughout, without being mentioned again. It's waiting for data.

Activating the Environment

Before any data can be loaded or any function can run, the environment needs to be deployed to runtime.

"Activate the NOVA2024 environment."

Confirm Operation - Activate Environment
Deploy NOVA2024 to runtime. This makes the environment available for data import and function execution.
[Verify →] [Approve] [Decline]

Approved. The environment status moves from Draft to Activated. The 12 master data tables and all allocation functions are now accessible for data loading.

Loading the Master Data

Before any transactional data can be imported or any allocation can run, the Association fields need their master data populated. Remember - these are the dimension fields where every value must exist in a reference table first. Without master data, a GL posting for account 70010000 or a transaction tagged to customer TECHFLOW would be rejected at import.

There are 12 master data tables to populate, plus 3 driver tables. Each one is a separate semicolon-delimited CSV file. The 12 master data tables in NOVA2024 are:

Scenario · Cost Center · Period · GL Account · Fiscal Year · Activity Driver · Resource Driver · Resource Pool · Customer · Service Activity · Service Line · Client Segment

The import sequence matters - reference tables that other tables depend on must go in first. GL Account, Customer, Resource Pool, and Service Activity need to be loaded before GL transaction data can reference them.

You attach each file via the paperclip icon and use a consistent prompt pattern:

"Import MasterData_Scenario.csv into the Master Data: Scenario table in NOVA2024."

Repeat for Cost Center, Period, Fiscal Year, Activity Driver, Resource Driver, Service Line, and Client Segment.

Loading the GL Source Data

With master data and driver data in place, the actual overhead cost postings can now be loaded into Stage 1: GL Accounts to Resource Pools.

NovaSpark's actuals are in a spreadsheet - 264 rows covering all 12 periods of FY2024. Click the paperclip icon and attach the file:

"Import NovaSpark_Actuals_2024.xlsx into Stage 1: GL Accounts to Resource Pools in NOVA2024. Map Account, Resource, AmountInLocalCurrency, FiscalYear, Period. Set Scenario = ACT for all rows."

264 rows imported. The source data is live and the model is ready to run.

No import screen. No schema wizard. No column mapping UI. One prompt and a file.

But when you open the function and inspect the data, something doesn't look right.

Debugging the Import

This is the moment that separates a conversational AI from a proper modelling assistant. The import ran - but the data isn't correct.

Three things are wrong:

  1. The FiscalYear field is blank - it wasn't set to 2024 despite the instruction
  2. The Account field (the GL account dimension) is empty - the account codes didn't map to the Association field
  3. The Code field, which should be the unique row key, was auto-generated as a concatenation of account + year + period (e.g. 70010000_2024_1) - that's not a meaningful key, and it would break updates if the file is re-imported

You flag all three directly in the chat:

"I can't see the fiscal year set to 2024 and also the GL account is not set. The code should not be a combination of account, year, and period."

Joule acknowledges the mapping errors, explains what went wrong, and re-executes the import with corrected field assignments:

This is worth noting because it reflects how a real build actually goes. The first import attempt wasn't wrong because of a bad prompt - it was a mapping ambiguity that Joule resolved incorrectly. The fix took one sentence. No manual data correction. No re-exporting the file. No navigating to an import configuration screen to adjust the column mapping. You described what was wrong in plain language, and Joule fixed it.

Running the Allocation Chain

One prompt to execute everything:

"Run all allocation functions in NOVA2024 in the correct order and show me the event log when complete."

Live streaming shows each stage execute in sequence. Activity chips update in real time as each function completes.

Understanding Your Model with Model Explorer

Before making any changes to a live model, you need to know what depends on what. Model Explorer answers that in one prompt.

"Show me the full dependency chain for the NOVA2024 allocation model. What would need to re-run if I changed the GL source data?"

Model Explorer maps the complete chain - Stage 1: GL Accounts to Resource Pools feeds all four Stage 2 allocation functions, which chain into Stage 3: Activities to Client Engagements (Time-Tracking). Changing the source data at Stage 1 requires a full re-run of every function downstream. Blast radius: HIGH. Joule recommends testing in a copy of the environment first.

You didn't ask about blast radius. Joule surfaced it because it understood the structural implication of the question - not just what you asked, but what you'd need to know before acting on it. For a model with five chained allocation functions, that kind of structural awareness isn't a nice-to-have. It's what makes the difference between a change that works and one that silently breaks something downstream.

One More Check: The Allocation Diagram

The finance director has an allocation flowchart in a presentation slide - drawn before PaPM was implemented. You screenshot it and attach it to the chat:

"Compare this diagram to what we've built in NOVA2024. Are there any flows in the diagram that we haven't implemented?"

Joule's Image/Vision capability reads the diagram and compares it against the live model configuration.

Most of it matches - but two gaps are flagged: a direct ManagementResource → TechFlow allocation path that doesn't exist in NOVA2024, and a design difference in how resource pool staging is modelled. Both are worth a conscious decision before the model goes live - one a potentially missing function, one a deliberate shortcut that works until mid-stage reporting becomes a requirement.

Generating the Documentation

The model is live. Now someone has to document it.

"Generate full documentation for NOVA2024. Include the environment purpose, each field and its business meaning, each function with its source and driver logic, the allocation flow from GL to client, and a validation checklist for after every run."

What comes back isn't a template. It's documentation generated directly from live model state - the actual fields, functions, and rules that exist in NOVA2024 right now. The function chain table, the driver basis for each stage, the validation checklist with specific things to check after every execution, the known limitations. Two navigation links at the bottom: one to the environment, one to the event log.

About the Example

This blog uses “NovaSpark Agency” as a fictional company to demonstrate how the Joule Universal Agent can generate models in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model (SAP PaPM). While the company, figures, and business data are fictional, the prompts are inspired by validated patterns and real-world SAP PaPM modeling practices.

 

To understand Joule capability, see the Introducing the Joule in Universal Model for SAP PaPM: When Your Model Finally Talks Back..

To understand Joule's Light or Intensive Usage Setup, see the Joule in SAP PaPM UM Cloud: Light or Intensive - Choose Right Before You Switch It On

entry.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model – Joule AI Agent: Environment and Process Management Capabilities
entry.content:
Hello, SAP Community members! 

We are excited to announce that Joule, the AI assistant embedded in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model (SAP PaPM Cloud SM), is now available in two additional applications: Environment and Process Management. 

In previous releases, Joule was available in Report Management, where it helped you analyze report data and generate insights. With this expansion, Joule is now your AI assistant in two additional applications, making it faster and more intuitive to navigate and accomplish tasks in Environment and Process Management. 

This blog post walks you through all Joule capabilities available on these two applications. If you are looking for the technical integration and setup steps (SAP AI Core, SAP Launchpad, BTP Destination), please refer to our previous blog post: 

SAP PaPM Cloud SM: Joule Setup Guide – BTP Configuration and Application 

General Joule Features 

Joule in Environment and Process Management is the same Joule available in Report Management — the conversation panel, its features, and the underlying AI are shared across all three applications. The following general features are available wherever Joule is enabled: 

  • Conversation History Sidebar – Browse, rename, delete, and resume past conversations; start a new one at any time. 
  • File Upload – Upload external files (up to 5 files, 5 MB each) and ask Joule to analyze them alongside your application data. 
  • Web Search – When activated by your administrator, Joule can search the internet and return cited results. 
  • Conversation Controls – Stop an ongoing response, switch to fullscreen mode, and use follow-up question suggestions. 
  • Your Joule Rules – Set personal instructions in the Joule settings — such as preferred language, response style, or level of detail — and Joule applies them automatically to every new conversation. 
  • Guided Help - When needed, Joule consults the official SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model documentation on the SAP Help Portal to answer your questions — giving you accurate, up-to-date guidance directly in the conversation, without leaving the application. 

For detailed descriptions of all these features, see: SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: Joule AI – Features and Capabilities in Report Management. 

Opening Joule and Choosing a Mode 

To open Joule in any Joule-enabled application, choose the Joule icon in the header toolbar. The Joule conversation panel opens on the right side of the screen. 

Before sending your first message, choose how Joule operates using the Ask/Act toggle in the message input area: 

  • Ask – Read-only mode. Joule answers your questions and retrieves information, but does not make any changes to your data. 
  • Act – Action mode. Joule can perform operations on your behalf, such as creating, editing, or deleting records. 

You can switch between Ask and Act at any point in the conversation. 

Notes:  

  • All actions performed by Joule in Act mode are bound by your existing user authorizations. Joule does not elevate your permissions — if you do not have access to a resource, Joule cannot act on it either. 
  • Actions performed in Act mode are done in the background. The screen does not refresh automatically, so refresh the Environment or Process Management screen to see the changes reflected in the list 

Joule Across Applications 

Joule is a single, unified AI assistant shared across all Joule-enabled applications in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model. Two capabilities highlight this: 

  • Shared conversation history – Every conversation you start in Joule is accessible from any Joule-enabled application. A conversation you began in Report Management can be continued from Environment or Process Management without losing context — and vice versa. 
  • Cross-application actions – You can ask Joule to perform actions on a different screen than the one you are currently on. For example, while working in Environment, you can ask Joule to create a process instance in Process Management — without navigating away from the current screen. 

Joule in the Environment Application 

The Environment screen displays the full list of available environments in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model, organized in a tree structure of nodes and environments. With Joule, you can explore, create, and manage both nodes and environments through natural language conversation. 

Asking Questions (Ask Mode) 

In Ask mode, Joule helps you explore and understand your environments and nodes. Ask it to list, filter, or describe environments based on any criteria. 

Example questions: 

  • "List all private environments." 
  • "Show me all environments in the RMS node." 
  • "List environments containing reports." 
  • "What actions can I perform in the Environment application?" 

The last example is particularly useful: ask Joule what it can do in the current application, and it will describe all available capabilities in full. 

Taking Actions (Act Mode) 

In Act mode, Joule can perform the following operations in the Environment application: 

  • Create environment/node – Specify the name, description, and other properties. You can create up to 50 environments in a single request; for larger quantities, Joule executes in multiple batches, each requiring your approval. 
  • Edit environment/node – Update the description of an environment or node. 
  • Move environment/node – Relocate an environment or node to a different parent node in the tree. 
  • Copy environment – Create a copy of an existing environment with a new ID and version. 
  • Mark as private or public – Change the access level between Public (visible to all users) and Private (restricted to authorized teams only). 
  • Assign a team – Set or update which teams are authorized to access a private environment. 
  • Delete environment/node – Remove an environment or an empty node. Because this is a destructive action, Joule lists exactly what will be deleted and asks for your explicit confirmation before proceeding. 

Note: Joule inherits your role assignments. For example, if you hold the ENVIRONMENTS_READ role only, Joule can view environments but cannot create, edit, or delete them. 

Joule in the Process Management Application 

The Process Management screen displays all process instances in a table, along with a Gantt diagram for visualizing timelines. With Joule, you can explore your process data and manage instances and activities through natural language conversation. 

Asking Questions (Ask Mode) 

In Ask mode, Joule helps you navigate and understand your process data. You can ask about templates, instances, activities, parameters, states, assigned teams, or any other process-related information. 

Example questions: 

  • "List all deployed process instances in the BAC environment, version 0001." 
  • "What is the current state of the Monthly_Close_May process?" 
  • "Show me all activities assigned to Team_A." 
  • "What are the parameters configured for process instance PROC06?" 

Taking Actions (Act Mode) 

In Act mode, Joule can perform the following operations on your process instances and activities: 

  • Create process instance from a template – Specify the template, process ID, description, type (Run or Simulation), and start date. You can create up to 50 instances at once; for larger quantities, Joule executes in multiple batches, each requiring your approval. 
  • Create process instance from an existing instance – Clone an existing process instance as the starting point for the new one, inheriting its configuration. 
  • Create process instance with adjusted selections and parameters – Fine-tune selections and parameter values when creating a new instance, without having to edit each field afterward through the UI. 
  • Edit an activity – Update the state, performer team, reviewer team, start date, or end date of an activity. 
  • Edit a process instance – Update the description, state, type (Run or Simulation), or start date of a process instance. 

Note: Joule inherits your role assignments. For example, if you hold the PROCESSES_OWN role only, Joule can manage only your own process instances. 

Closing Thoughts 

Joule in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model is now available across Report Management, Environment and Process Management applications. All capabilities are authorization-aware and operate within your existing user permissions. 

Whether you are setting up new environments for a planning cycle, managing process instance activities, or analyzing report data, Joule is there to help you work faster and more confidently — all through natural language. 

Useful Links 

Blog Posts: 

  • SAP PaPM Cloud SM: Joule Setup Guide – BTP Configuration and Application Settings 
  • SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: Joule AI – Features and Capabilities in Report Management 
  • SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: Introducing the AI Conversation Monitor 

Help Portal:  

  • Joule in Standard Model
  • Joule in Environment  
  • Joule in Process Management  
  • Joule in Report Management 

Stay tuned — we will continue expanding Joule capabilities across SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model. Thank you for reading!

entry.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model: What’s New as of 2026-10-06
entry.content:
Hi everyone! 👋

SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model just got a meaningful upgrade – and this release has something for nearly everyone. Whether you're a modeler looking to speed up your rule iteration cycles, a data manager who regularly loads business data from spreadsheets, or an integration specialist connecting new data sources, this latest update brings improvements that fit your day-to-day work.

This release introduces five new features:

  • A {refresh} placeholder that lets you embed a refresh button directly into any report tab
  • Bulk record duplication so you can copy multiple data entries at once
  • A new Joule capability to import CSV and XLSX files straight into your model through a natural conversation
  • A brand-new “BDC Data Product” connection type for consuming governed, harmonized data from SAP Business Data Cloud
  • The Run After Save toggle that automatically initiates a rule run every time you save. Together with story filter propagation this ensures that runs always process exactly the data you're looking at.

Here's the full rundown.

 

Joule in Universal Model

 

Import Spreadsheet Data into Your SAP PaPM Model Directly from Joule

Working with business data almost always starts with a spreadsheet. Whether it’s a fresh list of cost center master data or a set of transactional figures ready to load into an activity, the journey from file to model has traditionally meant multiple steps across different application screens.

With new enhancements for Joule in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model, that journey just got a lot shorter. You can now upload a CSV or XLSX file directly in your Joule conversation and ask it to import the data into the appropriate model entity or activity – no manual file preparation, no screen-switching.

 

What This Feature Does

The Import File capability lets you bring tabular data from XLSX or CSV files into your Universal Model through a natural conversation with Joule. You describe what you want to do, attach your file, and Joule takes care of the rest – checking that your data matches the target structure, transforming it if necessary, and confirming the outcome.

This benefits modelers and key users who regularly update master data in model entities or load transactional data into activities. Instead of navigating the import screens manually, you describe the task to Joule and let it handle the details.

The feature supports two import paths:

  • Model Entity import – loads master data into a model entity
  • Activity import – loads transactional data into a function-type activity with import enabled

 

Example

Imagine that you receive a spreadsheet containing new master data that needs to be loaded into your model.

Instead of manually preparing and importing the file through multiple application screens, you can upload the CSV or XLSX file directly to Joule and ask it to import the data into the appropriate model entity or activity. Joule guides you through the process, validates the information, and keeps you informed of the progress as the import is performed.

 

How It Works

  1. Open Joule and start a conversation.
  2. Upload a CSV or XLSX file.
  3. Describe the task you want to perform, such as importing master data or transaction data into a model entity or an activity.
  4. Joule analyzes the file and creates a plan to complete the requested task.
  5. Follow the progress in real time as Joule processes the request.
  6. Review the results and continue the conversation for additional actions or analysis.

For more information on the configuration, see Import File documentation in the SAP Help Portal.

 

What Else Is New in Joule

Import File is the centerpiece of this release, but it brings several other improvements to how Joule works in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model.

Aside from the Import File feature, the new release also includes real-time progress updates so you can follow every step as Joule works through your request, code execution for on-the-fly data transformation and calculation, and smarter task planning that shows you a visible checklist for multi-step operations.

Multiple AI agents can now work simultaneously on complex requests, and Joule handles longer conversations more reliably by preserving context across extended exchanges. Two new workflow skills – Import Data and Import Data Activity – join the ten skills from the previous release. New enhancements also include support for more AI models (including OpenAI GPT-5.5 and Google Gemini 3.5 Flash via a custom Destination connection), custom user settings so you can set behavioral preferences that Joule follows consistently, and improved response controls that focus Joule’s output on task-relevant information.

Together, these additions make Joule a more capable partner for the kinds of complex, multi-step analytical and modeling work that SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud users do every day.

For full technical details, see our blog post: Prompting Techniques for Joule in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model.

 

Model

Introducing New Connection Type: BDC Data Product

Universal Model now supports a new connection type: BDC Data Product. This connection allows users to consume governed, harmonized data products from SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) installed via SAP HANA Cloud or an existing space in SAP Datasphere.

Data products are read directly from the target HANA schema where they are installed. To maintain data governance and access restrictions, the required privileges must be granted to the technical schema of Universal Model, enabling it to access and read the underlying data records. This approach is similar to HANA Schema connections.

To learn more about the usage of the “BDC Data Product” connection type, see: BDC Data Product in the SAP Help Portal and SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model: Consuming Data Products from SAP BDC on SAP Community.

 

Data Screen

Duplicate Multiple Data Records in the Application Screens

Working with large data sets is now more efficient. You can duplicate multiple selected records at once directly in the Data screen, Report screen, and Model screen.

This enhancement helps streamline data maintenance tasks and speeds up the creation of related records, especially when working with multiple similar data entries.

 

Example

Imagine you have a set of data records in a model entity that define allocation parameters for a specific cost object. You need to create similar records for a second cost object with the same field structure but different key values.

Instead of building each record from scratch, the system generates duplicates of each selected record, pre-populating all available fields with the original values.

 

How It Works

  1. From the Data screen, select one or more records that you want to duplicate.
  2. Choose Create. The system generates draft copies of the selected records and automatically populates all available fields with values from the original records. The newly created drafts are highlighted in blue, indicating that they have not yet been saved.
  3. Review the duplicated records and make any necessary changes, such as updating key values or other fields.
  4. Save the drafts to create new records or discard them if they are no longer needed.

 

For more information about the procedure, see Duplicate Data.

 

Report Screen

 

Add a Refresh Button in Your Report with the {refresh} Placeholder

Have you ever wanted to give report viewers a quick way to reload the current report window – right from inside the report content itself? With the new {refresh} placeholder in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud, you can embed a Refresh button directly into any Report tab text. No configuration overhead, no custom scripting. Just add the placeholder, save the tab, and the button appears. In this post, we’ll walk through what the feature does, how to use it, and how to tailor the button’s appearance to match your reporting context.

 

What This Feature Does

The {refresh} placeholder is a new dynamic element for the Report Editor in the Universal Model. When you add it to the text of a Report tab, it renders as a clickable Refresh button in the saved (read-only) view. Clicking the button reloads the current Report window – the same behavior as a browser page refresh for that tab.

This feature is especially useful when you want to give key users a clear, self-service way to reload data without navigating away from the report. It’s also a practical companion to other dynamic placeholders like {username}, which the Report Editor already supports.

 

A Practical Example

Example 1: A Basic Refresh Button

Imagine you’re editing a Report tab that displays cost allocation results. You want viewers to be able to reload the data with a single click, without searching for a browser button or navigating away.

In the Report tab’s text editor, add the following placeholder where you want the button to appear:

{refresh}

Save the tab. In the saved view, the placeholder is no longer visible as raw text; it renders as a Refresh button.

When a user clicks the button, the current Report window reloads.

 

Example 2: A Custom-Styled Refresh Button

The default button works fine, but you may want it to stand out visually – for example, to match a report’s color scheme, or to signal an important action clearly.

You can customize the button’s label and appearance using inline styles and a label text:

{refresh style="background: red; color: white"}Reload Results{/refresh}

This renders a Refresh button with a red background, white text, and the custom label “Reload Results”.

Save the tab and reopen it. The custom style and label are preserved. Clicking the styled button reloads the report window, exactly as the default button does.

For full technical details, see the Report Screen documentation in the SAP Help Portal.

 

Run After Save and Story Filter Propagation in SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model

Developing and refining dynamic rules often involves frequent adjustments and validations. With the new Run After Save feature, active rules automatically run whenever you successfully save your changes. This seamless experience lets you move directly from editing to reviewing results, helping you work more efficiently and maintain your momentum.

 

What This Feature Does

The Run After Save toggle is now available as an optional setting on the Dynamic Rules screen. When you turn it on, every successful active-rule save automatically initiates the same run as the existing Run button, without an additional click.

Alongside this feature, the story filter propagation is now an official, fully supported behavior. When you apply story filters in a show report, those filters are now passed as field selections to runnable functions – whether you run them manually, via Run After Save, or through an automatic writer run initiated by data changes in a show element. Now, it is built in for all dynamic rule runs without any activities.

If you use Writer functions that run automatically when show element data changes, you can now configure a “Run After Save” relation type on a model entity. This relation type lets the Writer function run automatically whenever you save data in the show report. Your current story filter selections are automatically passed to the Writer function.

 

Scenario 1: Using the Run After Save Toggle

Imagine you are fine-tuning allocation rules in a rule element embedded in a show report. You are making small adjustments (e.g., changing driver values, tweaking conditions), and after each save, you want to immediately see the updated allocation results. Now, you can turn on Run After Save once at the start of your session and let it do that for you.

When you choose Save or Save All, the system automatically runs the same target as your Run button: The selected runnable activity if an activity target is in use, or the runtime function run otherwise. The layout stores your toggle setting, so if you use a saved report layout with Run After Save turned on, it restores that state when the layout loads.

What you see after the run is complete: The results in the show element update, exactly as they would after a manual run. If the automatic run fails after a successful save, the UI shows a causal message – for example, “Rule saved, but automatic run failed” – so you always know where the process stopped.

 

Scenario 2: Story Filters Propagated to Rule Element Run

Imagine you have a show report with story filters applied – for example, filtering to a specific cost center group. You run an Allocation function from the rule element embedded in that report. You want the function to process only the data that matches your active story filter selection, not the full dataset.

Now both the manual run and the automatic run after save in that rule element pass your current story filter selections as field selections in the run payload. The function processes only the matching data. After the run, the corresponding event log entries record which story filter values were applied.

This means, what you see in the show element is exactly what got processed.

Note
Story filter values that you have typed but not yet confirmed (not applied) are not included. The run always uses the currently applied filter values.

 

Scenario 3: Automatic Writer Run with Story Filter Propagation

Imagine your model has an input function that feeds into an allocation function through a writer. Users enter data directly into a show element in a report and expect the downstream allocation to update automatically when they save.

You can now configure a “Run After Save” relation type on the model entity that links the show element’s function to the Writer function. Once that relation is in place, every time a user saves data in the show report, the Writer function starts running automatically.

The story filters that the user currently has applied in the report travel with the writer run as field selections – consistent with how manual runs work. After the run, a Run After Save event appears in the event log with the run status, the Writer function that ran, and the story filter values that were applied.

For full technical details, see the Dynamic Rule Screen documentation in the SAP Help Portal.

 

That's what's new in SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model – five focused improvements that reduce friction, open up new data connectivity options, and make iterative modeling work feel a lot more fluid. We'd love to hear how you're using them. To stay on top of future releases, visit the What's New viewer, and explore more blog posts on the SAP Community using the tag PaPMCloudUMWhatsNew.

entry.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: What's New as of 2026-10-06?
entry.content:
Greetings, SAP Community! 👋 

We are back with the latest What's New updates for SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model. This round of improvements covers a lot of ground – and if you work with Joule, Modeling, or Process Management on a regular basis, you will likely feel the difference. 

Joule keeps growing – it now covers two more application screens. The Properties panel in Modeling opens the moment you select a node. You can delete process run data without removing the instance itself. And notification preferences have gotten a lot more specific. Whether you spend most of your time in Environment, Process Management, or Modeling, this update has something for you. Here is what has changed 📢

 

Joule 

Joule Now Available in Environment and Process Management 

Until now, business users could make use of Joule to help them with their reports. With this enhancement, Joule assistance is no longer limited to Report Management. Now Joule also supports the Environment and Process Management applications.  

Imagine asking Joule about pending process activities, cloning last month's process instance, and checking your environment setup. That is now possible. More than that, Joule in Standard Model can provide information and perform supported actions across all three applications – you don’t need to navigate to a specific application before asking. 

In the Environment application, Joule can provide information about existing environments and nodes. Use Act mode to create, edit, move, or delete them through conversation. Joule asks for your confirmation before performing irreversible actions such as deletion.  

 

In Process Management, Joule covers process templates, instances, activities, parameters, and selections. In Act mode, you can create a new process instance from a template – including custom selections and parameters in a single instruction – or clone an existing instance as the basis for a new run. You can also edit existing process instances and activities.  

 

For more information about Joule and its capabilities in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Standard Model, see Joule in Environment and Joule in Process Management in the SAP Help Portal. 

For a detailed walkthrough and examples, see SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model – Joule AI Agent: Environment and Process Management Capabilities.  

Ask Joule What You Can Do and How 

Finding out what is available on a given screen – and how to use it – often means leaving the application to search the SAP Help Portal manually. That is no longer the case. 

Joule now draws on built-in documentation from the SAP Help Portal for SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model. You can ask Joule what actions are available on a screen, how to perform them, and which roles are required – and get step-by-step answers that reference the actual UI elements and flows. 

Note 

This capability is currently available for the following applications: 

  • Environment 
  • Process Management 
  • Report Management 

For more information about Joule and its capabilities in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Standard Model, see Joule in Standard Model in the SAP Help Portal. 

Track Joule Conversation from Creation to Deletion 

If you use the Application Monitor or Process Monitor to review system events, you can now identify actions performed on Joule conversations more easily. 

Three new run types are available: 

  • Joule Conversation Creation: Logged when a conversation with Joule is initiated. 
  • Joule Conversation Renaming: Logged when a Joule conversation is renamed. 
  • Joule Conversation Deletion: Logged when a Joule conversation is deleted. 

Dedicated run types help you quickly identify and review Joule conversation activities in your monitoring screens.  

For more information, see Event Status and Run Types, Application Monitor, and Process Monitor in the SAP Help Portal. 

 

System - AI Conversation Monitor 

Review Action Results Directly on the Screen 

When managing Joule conversations, it is helpful to see the outcome of an action where you perform it. While toast messages provide quick feedback, it is also important to have those actions recorded and available for later review.  

With this enhancement, the Message Log in the AI Conversation Monitor now displays the results of upload, download, and delete actions, allowing you to review the results directly where the actions are performed.  

 When you need additional details, you can also review the events logged in the Application Monitor. These events are recorded under the following run types:  

  • Joule Conversation Upload  
  • Joule Conversation Download  
  • Joule Conversation Deletion

Together, the Message Log and Application Monitor help you review action results and access the corresponding monitoring records when needed.  

New to the AI Conversation Monitor? Refer to AI Conversation Monitor in the SAP Help Portal for an overview of the feature, prerequisites, and procedures for the available actions. For more information and an end-to-end scenario, see SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: Introducing the AI Conversation Monitor.  

 

Modeling 

Properties Open Automatically in Modeling 

Imagine you're working through a model and reviewing mappings and configuration settings. As you move between a Model Table, a Calculation function, and Process Templates, accessing its settings requires two separate actions: selecting the node and opening the Properties panel.  

With this enhancement, the Properties panel opens automatically when you select a node in the Modeling area. Whether you're reviewing a field, updating a parameter, or configuring a function, the relevant settings are available right away.  

The same behavior applies when you:  

  • Add a node from the palette  
  • Copy and paste a node  
  • Select a node from the modeling search results  

If the Properties panel is already open, it automatically updates to display the settings of the newly selected node.  

This makes it easier to review configuration details across connected modeling functions and stay focused on understanding and refining your model. 

Manage Fields Directly in "From" Rules 

When configuring the From rules in Join and Model Join functions, you often need to review or adjust how fields are assigned between join rule types. With this enhancement, you can now view and maintain these assignments directly in the Fields section of the Properties panel.  

This makes it easier to validate the structure of your join results while configuring the model.  

For more information, see Join Rule Types in the SAP Help Portal. 

Expand Your Result Model Table Options with Model Table HANA 

You can now select a Model Table HANA function in the Result Model Table of supported processing functions. 

Previously, Model Table HANA functions were not available as result model table options. With this enhancement, you can choose a Model Table HANA function as the result destination for Allocation, Calculation, Derivation, Transfer Structure, Join, View, and Iterative View functions. 

Instead of introducing an additional function to store results, you can define the target table directly in the processing function configuration, giving you more control over how and where your model results are stored. 

For more information, see Use Model Table HANA as Result Model Table. 

 

Process Management 

Delete Process Data Without Deleting Process Instances 

Sometimes, you want to remove the results of a process run without removing the process instance itself. For example, you may no longer need the generated data, but you still want to keep the process instance available for monitoring, auditing, or just for future reference.  

With this enhancement, you can now use the new Delete Process Data action in Process Management to delete process-related data generated by functions assigned to execution activities in one or more selected process instances while the selected instances are retained.  

The new Delete Process Data action is available in the Edit section of Process Management.  

 

 

Sample Scenario 

Consider a process instance that has already been run and generated process data. Before using Delete Process Data, the generated process data is available in the system. After the action, the process data generated is deleted, while the process instance remains available in Process Management.  

 

 

Confirmation Before Deletion

Before the deletion starts, the system displays a confirmation dialog so you can review and confirm the action.

Additional Option for Deleting Process Instances

You also have more flexibility when deleting process instances. The enhanced Delete Process Instance action now includes an Also delete associated process data option.  

This option lets you choose whether to:  

  • delete only the selected process instances; or  
  • delete both the selected process instances and their associated process data in a single step.  

 For more information,  check our SAP Help Portal documentation:  

  • Process Management  
  • Delete Process Data  
  • Delete Process Instance  

Receive Notifications for Due Activities 

Keeping track of upcoming activities is important when actions must be completed before a deadline.   

With this enhancement, you can receive both in-app and email notifications 3 days before an activity's due date and again on the due date itself. The due date is determined based on the activity's end date.  

Sample In-App Notifications for Due Process Activities

Notifications are sent when a process instance is in the Deployed state, and the associated activities have not yet been completed. Both activity performers and reviewers can receive these reminders. Email notifications include a direct link to the relevant activity, allowing you to access the activity and take the required action.  

This improves the visibility of pending process activities and helps you stay informed about upcoming deadlines. 

For more information, see Notifications and Dual Control in the SAP Help Portal. 

 

User Profile 

Notification Preferences by Type and Environment 

Notifications help you stay informed about changes across your environment, but the notifications you want to receive may differ depending on your role and responsibilities.  

Previously, notification preferences could only be managed by notification channel, allowing you to activate or deactivate In-App and Email notifications.  

With this enhancement, you can now configure notification preferences for individual notification types when your administrator allows users to manage those settings.  

There are two parts to the new experience.  

First, choose your notification types 

In Notification Types, you can set your in-app and email preferences separately for: 

  • Activity changes 
  • Process changes 
  • Scheduled jobs 
  • Team changes 
  • Private environment changes 

Your administrator still determines which settings you can manage. If a setting has been predefined by your administrator, its checkbox is not editable. 

Second, choose the environment scope 

In Environments, you can decide where your notification settings apply: 

  • All environments 
  • Selected environments 
  • All environments except the ones you specify 

Any notification settings configured by your administrator are not affected by the environment settings you choose.  

Together, these options give you more control over your personal notification preferences while still respecting the settings managed by your administrator.  

For more information, see:

  • For users: Notifications - Learn how to manage your notification preferences in User Preferences.   
  • For administrators: Global Notification Settings - Learn how to configure notification settings at the global level.   
  • For a detailed walkthrough: SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model: Notification Management in User Preferences – Explore an end-to-end example of how user notification preferences and global notification settings work together. 

That covers the highlights for SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model in this round 🌟 

To always see the latest updates in one place, visit our official What's New on SAP Help Portal. You can also browse previous What's New blog posts on the SAP Community using the #PaPMCloudSMWhatsNew tag.

Until next month! 🚀

entry.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model: Consuming Data Products from SAP BDC
entry.content:
SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model (SAP PaPM Cloud UM) introduces the BDC Data Product connection type, enabling you to access SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) harmonized data products through a Targeted HANA Schema maintained within this connection. This allows you to use standardized, business-ready data directly in your modeling projects without custom integration work.

Before you dive in, take a moment to review the key terms used throughout this documentation. Understanding these will help you navigate the content more easily. See, Application Help for Universal Model – BDC Data Product

Prerequisites

  • You must have an SAP BDC Data Product installed in your SAP HANA Cloud or SAP Datasphere.
    For more information, see Access and Query a Data Product in SAP HANA Cloud, Installing Marketplace Data Products - SAP Datasphere.
  • You must have the required roles for the creation of connection. See, Manage Connections.
  • You must have an Uploaded CSN Interop JSON or BDC API Resource ORD ID for fetching the metadata, allowing the application to locate and pull the correct blueprint of Data Products.
    For more information, see Data Products.

Setting Up the BDC Data Product Connection

Setting up a BDC Data Product connection will feel familiar if you've worked with HANA Schema connections. It shares the same core fields: Connection ID, Description, and Tenant Specific Configuration, with the addition of Default Key

Importing the BDC Data Product Metadata

To complete the connection setup, import the metadata of the BDC Data Product you want to consume by uploading its CSN Interop JSON file. This file contains the data product structure including its entities, field names, data types, and relationships, and can be downloaded from the SAP API Business Hub - Data Products.

See the image below where you can download the CSN Interop JSON. Sample data product here: Data Product General Ledger Account

Once uploaded, pressing Import BDC Metadata will now load all available models from the CSN Interop JSON file, including their fields, relations, and other defined structures. From here, you can configure the models depending on your use case, selecting the specific fields, relations, and other components you need.

You can also rename the Target Function Name of each model to align with how you want to reference the Data Product table in your modeling. Please take note that these imported data products are generated as read-only Model HANA Functions, which can be activated and used for data access in your modeling projects.

The image above shows an example of a BDC Data Product model displaying its available fields and relations. All of these are based on the structure defined in the CSN Interop JSON file, which SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model automatically translates into a modeling UI that you can configure and use directly in your modeling.

Once you have configured your models by mapping the necessary fields and applying the required relations, you can proceed with Sync Model to synchronize the connection and Activate to make the data product available. After a successful activation, the BDC Data Product data is now ready to be consumed directly in your modeling projects within SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model.

Common Warnings and Errors

As you set up and configure your BDC Data Product connection, you may encounter some warnings and errors along the way. This section covers the most common ones to help you quickly identify and resolve them.

Warning: Schema Does Not Expose BDC Data Product Objects

This warning may appear during the creation of your BDC Data Product connection when the selected or synced model from the BDC Data Products is not detected in the Target HANA Schema. This typically means the Target HANA Schema does not have the corresponding BDC Data Product installed or is not accessible by the technical schema of SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model.

To resolve this, make sure the Target HANA Schema you have configured contains the BDC Data Products you intend to consume and is accessible to SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model.

Error: BDC Virtual Table or Consumption View Not Found

This error occurs during Activation when SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model searches for the synced or selected BDC Data Product from the created connection but cannot find it in the Target HANA Schema. During activation, Universal Model looks for the corresponding virtual table or consumption view of the BDC Data Product in the Target HANA Schema. When nothing is found, the activation fails with this error.

To resolve this, make sure the correct Target HANA Schema is maintained where the BDC Data Product is installed and visible to SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model.

All right, that will be it for now! With the BDC Data Product connection type now available in SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model, consuming harmonized, business-ready data from SAP Business Data Cloud has never been more straightforward. By leveraging the CSN Interop JSON, you can quickly set up your connection, configure your models, and start using BDC Data Products directly in your calculations. See you again on my next blog post!

entry.title: A Practical Guide to Manage Tenant Connections in SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model
entry.content:
As SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model landscapes grow, organizations typically operate across multiple tenants such as Development (DEV), Quality Assurance (QAS), and Production (PRD). While transporting environments between tenants is a standard practice, managing HANA Schema Connections across these environments can become a maintenance challenge.

A common question is:

How can you transport models across tenants without reconfiguring HANA Schema Connections after every transport?

The solution is Manage Tenant Connections, this feature allows you to create and maintain HANA Schema connection that is tenant-specific. By defining tenant-specific mappings, you can transport models between tenants without repeatedly updating connection settings. Each PaPM Cloud tenant can then independently control which physical HANA schema the connection points to.

 

Why Use Manage Tenant Connections?

By using tenant-specific connections, you can:

  • Keep the same HANA Schema Connection name across multiple tenants.
  • Reduce maintenance after transports.
  • Configure schema assignments independently per tenant.
  • Minimize the risk of errors caused by manual connection updates after transports.
  • Prepare your landscape for future changes without modifying existing models.

Bottom line: Consistent models, flexible schema assignments, and fewer deployment risks.

 

How It Works?

Imagine you have developed a model that uses the HANA Schema Connection CONSALES to read from or write to the SALES table.

By setting the connection's Tenant Specific property to Yes, each tenant can maintain its own schema assignment through Manage Tenant Connections.

In the Source Tenant, CONSALES points to FIN_SRC HANA Schema, while in the Target Tenant, CONSALES points to FIN_TGT HANA Schema. When the model is transported, nothing in the model needs to change. The same connection, table reference, and business logic are reused, while PAPM automatically resolves the correct schema based on the tenant-specific configuration. 

 

How to Use Manage Tenant Connections?

Now that we've covered the concept and benefits of Manage Tenant Connections, let's walk through a practical example.

Disclaimer: The screenshots and configuration values shown in this guide are for illustration purposes only. Connection names, schema names, descriptions, and other values are sample data intended to demonstrate the setup process and may differ from your actual system landscape.

 

Prerequisite:

Before proceeding, ensure the following requirements are met:

  • You must have an access to Administration, Connection Management and Manage Tenant Connections. Refer to Role Templates in Universal Model
  • SAP Cloud Universal Model have the access to read or write in the HANA Schema. Refer to Database Administration in BYOD SAP HANA Cloud and Database Administration in BYOD SAP Datasphere
  • The HANA Schema Connection must be configured with Tenant Specific = Yes. Refer to Manage Connections: HANA Schema
  • The HANA Schema Connection Name must be identical across all tenants

 

Source Tenant Configuration

Step 1: Ensure Tenant-Specific Is Enabled for the HANA Schema Connection

Before configuring Manage Tenant Connections, verify that the HANA Schema Connection is configured with Tenant Specific = Yes. This setting allows each tenant to maintain its own schema mapping while using the same connection name across the landscape.

When reviewing the HANA Schema Connection:

a. Navigate to Manage Environment > Environment > Connections

b. Open the HANA Schema Connection that will be used by the model.

c. Verify that Tenant Specific is set to Yes.

Important: The connection name must remain identical across all tenants. When Tenant Specific is enabled, the schema assignment is maintained separately through Manage Tenant Connections, allowing the same model to be transported without modifying connection references.

 

Step 2: Configure Manage Tenant Connections

a. Navigate to Administration > Manage Tenant Connections

b. Select Create.

c. The Environment field is optional. Note that only activated environments will be displayed in the value help. Select HANA Schema as the Connection Target Type, then click Continue.

e. Enter the required values

Attribute

Value

Connection

Provide the HANA Schema Connection

Description

Optional

Target HANA Schema

Provide the Target HANA Schema for the Source Tenant

After saving, the CONSALES connection is mapped to the FIN_SRC schema.

 

Step 3: Export the Environment

Export the environment from the source tenant using the standard SAP PaPM Cloud export process. For detailed guidance, refer to the SAP Help documentation: Export Environment

 

Target Tenant Configuration

Step 1: Import the Environment to the target tenant

Import the environment to the target tenant using the standard SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model Import process. For detailed guidance, refer to the SAP Help documentation: Import Environment. At this stage, the environment can remain inactive.

 

Step 2: Configure Manage Tenant Connections in the target tenant

Before activating the imported environment, create the corresponding tenant connection in the target tenant.

  1. Navigate to Administration > Manage Tenant Connections.
  2. Select Create.
  3. The Environment field is optional. Note that only activated environments will be displayed in the value help. Select HANA Schema as the Connection Target Type, then click Continue.
  4. Use the same connection name used in the source tenant and specify the target schema.

Attribute

Value

Connection

Provide the HANA Schema Connection

Description

Optional

Target HANA Schema

Provide the Target HANA Schema for the Target Tenant

This is the key benefit of tenant-specific connections wherein the model remains identical while each tenant controls its own schema assignment.

 

IMPORTANT NOTE:

The Target HANA Schema maintained in the HANA Schema Connection serves as the connection definition; however, when Tenant Specific = Yes is enabled, the actual runtime schema for each tenant is controlled by Manage Tenant Connections. Therefore, always check Administration > Manage Tenant Connections to confirm the effective schema assignment.

 

Step 3: Activate The Environment and Perform Validation

After configuring the tenant connection:

  1. Activate the imported environment.
  2. Execute a process that uses the HANA Schema Connection (for example, a Reader or Writer function).
  3. Verify that the operation uses the expected target schema.

Test Result:

In this example, a Writer function was executed after activation.

Although the model continued to reference the CONSALES connection, the target tenant's Manage Tenant Connections configuration redirected the operation to FIN_TGT. As expected, the data was successfully written to FIN_TGT.SALES without requiring any modifications to the transported model.

FIN_SRC.SALES

 

FIN_TGT.SALES

 

Final Thoughts:

Manage Tenant Connections is a simple yet powerful feature that helps organizations streamline their SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model. If you're working with a multi-tenant SAP PaPM Cloud landscape, implementing tenant-specific connections can save time, reduce manual effort, and make your deployments more reliable.

Have you already started using Manage Tenant Connections in your SAP PaPM Cloud projects? Share your experiences and tips in the comments below.

Reference

SAP Application Help: Universal Model > Manage Tenant Connections > HANA Schema

SAP Learning: Managing Tenant Connections

entry.title: Agentic AI Needs an Environment: Lessons from PaPM and ERP Controlling
entry.content:
For an AI to be truly agentic, it needs an environment to work in. To me, this is almost self-evident.

Connecting an LLM to data is not enough. The environment needs state, business logic, functions the agent can call, and a way to receive feedback from a human. Only then can the AI do more than answer a question. It can move toward a goal: look at what is happening, decide what to do next, run the right function, inspect the result, spot a problem, form a hypothesis, and test it.

By this definition, both a calculation model in SAP Profitability and Performance Management (PaPM) and the Controlling module in ERP can serve as environments for agentic AI.

1. The PaPM calculation model as an environment

In PaPM, the calculation is stored in a narrative form. Functions embed the methodology, and the methodology consists of a preparation phase and the factor analysis calculation itself.

So where does the agentic part come in? I don’t see our agent as a chat that looks at a final table and writes a nicely worded report. Imagine it receives a task: run the calculation and analyze the significant variances for a specific production order. The agent then works out the steps on its own. It prepares the required data, runs the right functions, executes the calculation, looks at the result, and only then starts analyzing. Along the way it can:

  • determine which preparation functions need to run,
  • execute the right sequence of functions,
  • retrieve the result,
  • walk through the final table and find significant variances,
  • identify which factor drove each variance,
  • trace back through the model and methodology to understand how the number was produced,
  • prepare a final report for the user.

Suppose the agent notices that the standard price differs sharply from the actual one. It digs into the drivers and finds that one factor is the number of hours: 170 working hours were expected, but only 10 hours were allocated to this production order.

Context matters here. We are looking at a single production order, but cost allocation happens during period-end closing. If more production orders had been closed in the period, the costs (specifically labor costs) would have been spread across them, and the result for this order would look different.

So the agent doesn’t just say, “You have 170 planned hours against 10 actual.” It explains why this affected the result and how the figure connects to the calculation methodology: the gap between expected and allocated hours changed the cost distribution and, in turn, the outcome of the factor analysis.

When the model isn’t enough

Sometimes the information inside the PaPM model is not sufficient to find the real cause. This is where I also see agentic behavior. The agent must not invent a cause and present it as fact. It should say something like:

“A possible reason is how the actual production time was recorded in ERP.” (a hypothesis)

Then it needs to figure out how to verify that hypothesis, and tell the human where to look:

“Check production order X in ERP. Review the confirmed production time and the source it came from in the calculation.”

The agent is no longer just answering a question. It is directing a person to what needs to be checked. The person goes to ERP, confirms or rejects the hypothesis, and the loop continues.

This points to an important architectural principle. ERP is our source of truth, so the LLM must never decide on its own that a hypothesis is a fact. Once a human confirms the cause, we can use that information going forward. And we don’t necessarily need to copy ERP data into PaPM or replicate anything. We can create a new view on the PaPM side that gives the agent access to the relevant ERP information. Next time, the agent can consult that source and include it in its analysis.

The full cycle looks like this:

calculation result → model analysis → missing information → hypothesis → next step → verification in ERP → human confirmation → new access to the needed information → next analysis with that context

That, for me, is where agentic AI appears. Not in the LLM’s ability to write fluent text, but in the agent’s ability to understand what to do next, what information it lacks, where to go, what to check, and how to continue once it has an answer. The agent can also do more than analyze a finished result. It can run the calculation itself by executing the sequence of methodology functions in PaPM.

2. The Controlling module in ERP

In ERP this is, in my view, even more obvious. The agent operates inside the system that is the source of truth. It knows which controlling tables exist, what they mean, how they relate, which processes exist, and which functions it can call. So it can perform concrete tasks, not just analyze:

  • create a cost center,
  • check an existing cost center,
  • validate an allocation function,
  • verify that data is configured correctly,
  • execute period-end closing steps,
  • work with reporting and the Review Booklet,
  • search for root causes of variances.

Period-end closing shows this best. The goal is simple to state: close the period. But that is not a single function call. It is a sequence of actions: check that all prerequisites are met, including settlement, then check the data, find errors or blockers, run the necessary functions, verify again, and move on.

When something goes wrong, the agent must decide what to do next. For example:

closing → error in allocation → analyze the allocation function → find a missing cost center → depending on what is being allocated, determine which master data is missing → fix it → rerun allocation → check the result → continue closing

This shows what agentic means: goal → planning → action → observe the outcome → decide what’s next → revise the plan if needed.

Our PaPM agent does exactly the same thing. The difference is only in which functions it runs. In ERP, they belong to a business process such as period closing. In PaPM, they belong to the calculation model, accessed through Joule for PaPM and then through Joule Work, a kind of universal workstation connected to the different systems in the landscape.

3. So what is the difference between PaPM and ERP?

For me, the difference is not that one scenario is agentic and the other isn’t. Both can be. The environments are simply different.

In ERP, the agent sits where the business state and the source of truth live, so it doesn’t need extra views to reach the root cause. In PaPM, the agent has the calculation model, methodology, functions, and results, but part of the information needed to explain a root cause lives in ERP. At some point the agent may conclude: “I understand the calculation, but I lack the information to explain the cause.” Then it has to go further.

Put simply:

  • ERP tells us what is happening in the business.
  • PaPM shows how the calculated result was produced.
  • The agent works out why the result looks the way it does, what is missing, and what to do next.

Why this is more than an “analytical assistant”

I wouldn’t call this agent merely an analytical assistant. Yes, it helps users with analytics, but the core idea is different.

Today, a person walks through multiple transactions, exports several Excel files, compares tables, calculates things, finds a variance, goes to another system to verify the cause, and finally assembles a report. The point of an agent is to take the human out of that routine sequence of actions.

The same goal applies to an agent handling period closing. Today a person runs the functions, checks the results, hunts for errors, and decides what to do next. The agent should do that work instead.

That is why I see no fundamental difference between these two flows:

closing → run allocation → check → run settlement → check → finish closing

run PaPM preparation phase → run calculation → review result → find variance → understand cause → request additional information → verify it → continue analysis

Behaviorally, it is the same logic: there is a goal, there is a set of available actions, and the agent chooses what to do next, observes the result, and continues.

This is also why I believe that preparing an important prerequisite for the calculation with a colleague was a real step forward. Yes, a person can walk through transactions and export a number of Excel files to build a report. But then the question is: why do we need an agent at all? The answer is that a person should no longer have to do this. The agent should own the whole process.

The idea may not have been fully understood at first, because it is somewhat indirect. I am not trying to build yet another chat that tells users a nice story about what happened. I want an assistant that performs the sequence of actions a human performs today.

The LLM is there to understand context, interpret information, form hypotheses, decide on next steps, and connect different sources. ERP and PaPM remain the systems that hold the business itself and the calculation logic.

That is why I see agentic AI as an intelligent layer on top of existing systems, not a replacement for them. That, in the end, is the whole point.
